questions.f: Prompt templates run in Lightning Experience on Professional, Enterprise and Unlimited editions with no add-on required.
questions.x: Prompt Builder needs Enterprise, Performance or Unlimited edition plus an Einstein or Agentforce add-on or Agentforce Foundations. Some template types need further add-ons.

questions.t: A single SOQL query can include at most 55 child-to-parent relationships and at most 20 parent-to-child relationships.
questions.f: A single SOQL query can include at most 20 child-to-parent relationships and at most 55 parent-to-child relationships.
questions.x: The ceiling is 55 for child-to-parent traversals and 20 for parent-to-child subqueries. Each type in a TYPEOF clause counts toward the limit, but reusing a relationship counts once.

questions.t: A hierarchical relationship is a special lookup that exists only on the User object, used for chains such as managers.
questions.f: A hierarchical relationship is a special lookup that can be added to any custom object to model parent-child chains.
questions.x: Hierarchical relationships are limited to User, which is how fields like Manager link one user to another. Other objects use standard lookup or master-detail fields.

questions.t: Custom objects on the detail side of a master-detail relationship can't use sharing rules, manual sharing or queues.
questions.f: Custom objects on the detail side of a master-detail relationship can use sharing rules and queues, but not manual sharing.
questions.x: Detail records inherit access from their master and have no owner of their own, so sharing rules, manual sharing and queues are all unavailable to them.

questions.t: Enabling person accounts requires the organization-wide default for contacts to be Controlled by Parent.
questions.f: Enabling person accounts requires the organization-wide default for contacts to be Private.
questions.x: Contacts must inherit access from their account before person accounts can be turned on. The other prerequisites are a business account record type and Read on contacts wherever profiles can read accounts.

questions.t: Person accounts can be enabled for customer Experience Cloud sites but not for partner sites.
questions.f: Person accounts can be enabled for partner Experience Cloud sites but not for customer sites.
questions.x: Person accounts work with customer-facing sites, which suits B2C self-service. Partner sites aren't supported for them.

questions.t: In Lightning lead conversion, a lead with a blank Company becomes a person account, and one with a Company becomes a business account.
questions.f: In Lightning lead conversion, a lead with a filled-in Company becomes a person account, and one with a blank Company becomes a business account.
questions.x: The Company field decides the account type on conversion: blank means an individual, so a person account is created. That's why separate lead record types and layouts are advised.

questions.t: In a SOQL query, the OFFSET clause can skip at most 2,000 rows.
questions.f: In a SOQL query, the OFFSET clause can skip at most 50,000 rows.
questions.x: OFFSET is capped at 2,000 rows, so it isn't suited to paging through large result sets. The 50,000 figure is the per-transaction cap on records retrieved by SOQL in Apex.

questions.t: Per the Winter '27 Apex guide, Apex at API version 67.0 or later runs in user context by default, enforcing the user's sharing and permissions.
questions.f: Per the Winter '27 Apex guide, Apex at API version 67.0 or later runs in system mode by default, ignoring the user's sharing and permissions.
questions.x: From API 67.0, Apex defaults to user context, applying sharing, field-level security and object permissions. Versions 66.0 and earlier default to system mode.

questions.t: Email verification for Experience Cloud sign-up is included, but SMS verification needs the Identity Verification Credits add-on.
questions.f: SMS verification for Experience Cloud sign-up is included, but email verification needs the Identity Verification Credits add-on.
questions.x: Verifying by email costs nothing extra. Sending codes by text message consumes Identity Verification Credits, which are bought as an add-on.

questions.t: If no default account is set for site self-registration and person accounts are enabled, Salesforce creates person accounts for new users.
questions.f: If no default account is set for site self-registration, Salesforce puts every new user's contact under one shared placeholder account it creates.
questions.x: Self-registration normally links new contacts to a configured default account. With none set, Salesforce falls back to person accounts, but only when the org has them enabled.

questions.t: A Login Discovery page runs an Apex class implementing Auth.LoginDiscoveryHandler, which can send one-time codes via Site.passwordlessLogin.
questions.f: A Login Discovery page runs an Apex class implementing Auth.RegistrationHandler, which can send one-time codes via Site.passwordlessLogin.
questions.x: LoginDiscoveryHandler's login method finds the user from the identifier and decides the challenge, such as a passwordless code or a redirect to an identity provider. RegistrationHandler is a different interface.

questions.t: A candidate who fails the CTA Architect Evaluation receives feedback and may re-register after six months.
questions.f: A candidate who fails the CTA Architect Evaluation receives feedback and may re-register after 30 days.
questions.x: The online evaluation has a six-month wait before another attempt. Passing it is what makes a candidate eligible for the Architect Review Board exam.

questions.t: Rescheduling the Architect Review Board exam without a fee requires at least 30 days' notice.
questions.f: Rescheduling the Architect Review Board exam without a fee requires at least 7 days' notice.
questions.x: Fee-free rescheduling needs 30 days' notice. The review board is currently held online until further notice.

questions.t: If an architect certification has lapsed for more than one maintenance cycle, the exam has to be retaken.
questions.f: If an architect certification has lapsed for more than one maintenance cycle, completing the missed maintenance badges reinstates it.
questions.x: A recently expired credential may be reinstated through a support case, though not guaranteed. Once it has lapsed beyond one cycle, the only route back is passing the exam again.

questions.t: A My Domain name can be 3 to 34 characters in production and sandboxes, but only 3 to 27 in a Developer Edition org.
questions.f: A My Domain name can be 3 to 63 characters in production and sandboxes, but only 3 to 27 in a Developer Edition org.
questions.x: Production and sandbox names allow up to 34 characters of letters, numbers and hyphens, and can't start with a hyphen. Developer Edition orgs are capped at 27.

questions.t: After a My Domain rename, only the most recent previous name redirects, so successive renames break older links.
questions.f: After a My Domain rename, every previous name keeps redirecting, so successive renames never break older links.
questions.x: Salesforce redirects just the last former hostname. Renaming twice leaves the oldest URLs broken, which is why hard-coded URLs need review.

questions.t: With enhanced domains, Experience Cloud sites are served at MyDomainName.my.site.com.
questions.f: With enhanced domains, Experience Cloud sites are served at MyDomainName.my.salesforce-sites.com.
questions.x: Enhanced domains put the My Domain name in every URL. Experience Cloud sites use my.site.com, while my.salesforce-sites.com is the format for Salesforce Sites.

questions.t: RFC 9700 requires public OAuth clients to use PKCE with the S256 method.
questions.f: RFC 9700 requires public OAuth clients to use PKCE with the plain method.
questions.x: The 2025 OAuth security best practice makes PKCE with S256 mandatory for public clients. The plain method is weaker and is forbidden outright in the OAuth 2.1 draft.

questions.t: An OAuth 2.0 refresh token is presented only to the authorization server, never to resource servers.
questions.f: An OAuth 2.0 refresh token is presented to resource servers in place of an access token once it expires.
questions.x: Refresh tokens are exchanged at the token endpoint for new access tokens. Resource servers accept only access tokens.

questions.t: Salesforce restricted creating new connected apps in Spring '26 and recommends external client apps for new integrations.
questions.f: Salesforce restricted creating new external client apps in Spring '26 and recommends connected apps for new integrations.
questions.x: External client apps are the recommended OAuth client registration going forward. New connected app creation has been restricted since Spring '26.

questions.t: The Salesforce OAuth JWT bearer flow never issues a refresh token, and scopes can't be requested in the assertion.
questions.f: The Salesforce OAuth JWT bearer flow issues a refresh token with each access token, and scopes are requested in the assertion.
questions.x: JWT bearer returns only an access token, with scopes coming from the app's policy or API Access Control. The server simply signs a new JWT when it needs another token.

questions.t: The OAuth username-password flow is blocked by default in orgs created in Summer '23 or later, though it can be re-enabled.
questions.f: The OAuth username-password flow is allowed by default in orgs created in Summer '23 or later, though admins can block it.
questions.x: Newer orgs start with the username-password flow blocked. Salesforce recommends keeping it and the user-agent flow blocked and using JWT bearer or client credentials instead.

questions.t: In the Salesforce client credentials flow, every access token carries the permissions of the app's designated run-as user.
questions.f: In the Salesforce client credentials flow, every access token carries the permissions of the admin who approved the app.
questions.x: The app is configured with a run-as user and tokens act with that user's access. Salesforce advises a dedicated integration user limited by permission sets.

questions.t: For an OpenID Connect Auth. Provider, Salesforce checks the ID token against the issuer and user-info response but doesn't verify its signature.
questions.f: For an OpenID Connect Auth. Provider, Salesforce verifies the ID token's signature before checking it against the issuer and user-info response.
questions.x: Signature validation isn't done automatically. If it matters, the registration handler should validate the token itself with Auth.JWTUtil.

questions.t: The Execute Registration As user for an Auth. Provider's registration handler needs the Manage Users permission.
questions.f: The Execute Registration As user for an Auth. Provider's registration handler needs the Modify All Data permission.
questions.x: The handler creates and updates users, so its run-as user needs Manage Users. A dedicated service account keeps registration working if an admin leaves.

questions.t: An Auth. Provider's consumer secret is replaced with a placeholder when retrieved through the Metadata API.
questions.f: An Auth. Provider's consumer secret is retrieved in plain text through the Metadata API, so it deploys with the definition.
questions.x: Since November 2022 retrievals mask the secret. Deployments have to restore it or it must be re-entered in Setup.

questions.t: Lightning Experience users get the App Launcher by default, while Classic users need the Use Identity Features permission.
questions.f: Classic users get the App Launcher by default, while Lightning Experience users need the Use Identity Features permission.
questions.x: The App Launcher is built into Lightning Experience. In Salesforce Classic it appears only for users granted Use Identity Features.

questions.t: Each Developer Edition org comes with five External Identity licenses.
questions.f: Each Developer Edition org comes with 100 External Identity licenses.
questions.x: Developer Edition includes five External Identity licenses for trying out customer identity. In production they are sold in blocks of active users.

questions.t: In inbound SSO, an external identity provider authenticates the user and Salesforce acts as the service provider.
questions.f: In inbound SSO, Salesforce authenticates the user as the identity provider and signs them in to third-party apps.
questions.x: Inbound means users arrive at Salesforce already authenticated by another IdP. Salesforce acting as the identity provider for other apps is outbound SSO.

questions.t: A Salesforce SAML configuration can match the incoming user by Salesforce username, Federation ID or User ID.
questions.f: A Salesforce SAML configuration can match the incoming user by email address, Federation ID or employee number.
questions.x: The SAML Identity Type setting offers exactly three keys: username, Federation ID and User ID. The value is read from the NameIdentifier or a named attribute.

questions.t: A user's Federation ID must be unique within an org, and a user present in several orgs should carry the same value in each.
questions.f: A user's Federation ID must be unique across all Salesforce orgs, so a user present in several orgs needs a different value in each.
questions.x: Uniqueness is enforced per org. Reusing the same Federation ID for one person across orgs lets a single IdP identity sign in everywhere.

questions.t: In a Salesforce SAML configuration, the Entity ID must match an Audience value in the IdP's assertion.
questions.f: In a Salesforce SAML configuration, the Entity ID must match the Issuer element in the IdP's assertion.
questions.x: The Entity ID identifies the org, usually its My Domain URL, and is checked against the assertion's Audience. The Issuer field is the one that must match the IdP's Issuer element.

questions.t: A Bulk API 2.0 ingest job accepts up to 150 MB of base64-encoded CSV, so Salesforce suggests raw uploads under 100 MB.
questions.f: A Bulk API 2.0 ingest job accepts up to 1 GB of base64-encoded CSV, so Salesforce suggests raw uploads under 750 MB.
questions.x: The cap is 150 MB after base64 encoding, which inflates data by about half. Keeping the raw file under 100 MB leaves room for that growth.

questions.t: Bulk API 2.0 ingest jobs draw on the 15,000 daily batches shared with Bulk API 1.0, but query jobs don't consume batches.
questions.f: Bulk API 2.0 query jobs draw on the 15,000 daily batches shared with Bulk API 1.0, but ingest jobs don't consume batches.
questions.x: Only ingest work counts against the shared batch allocation. Query jobs have their own limits of 10,000 jobs and 1 TB of results per rolling 24 hours.

questions.t: A Bulk API 2.0 ingest job can stay open for at most 24 hours, and its results can be retrieved for 7 days after completion.
questions.f: A Bulk API 2.0 ingest job can stay open for at most 7 days, and its results can be retrieved for 24 hours after completion.
questions.x: Open jobs must be closed within a day. Once a job finishes, its success and failure results stay available for seven days before the job is deleted.

questions.t: A Pub/Sub API subscribe call can request at most 100 events in total across its fetch requests.
questions.f: A Pub/Sub API subscribe call can request at most 2,000 events in total across its fetch requests.
questions.x: Requests above 100 events are treated as 100. The client asks for more once it has processed what it received.

questions.t: gRPC caps a Pub/Sub API publish request at 4 MB, and Salesforce recommends keeping batches at or below 3 MB.
questions.f: gRPC caps a Pub/Sub API publish request at 1 MB, and Salesforce recommends keeping batches at or below 500 KB.
questions.x: A request over 4 MB fails and closes the stream, so batches of about 3 MB and 200 events are advised. The 1 MB figure is the size limit for a single event.

questions.t: Pub/Sub API subscriptions are pull-based: the client sends a FetchRequest saying how many events it can handle.
questions.f: Pub/Sub API subscriptions are push-based: the server streams each new event as soon as it is published, without client flow control.
questions.x: Clients request a number of events and the server delivers up to that count before waiting for the next request. This flow control protects slow consumers during spikes.

questions.t: The query optimizer considers a custom index when a filter matches under 10% of records, capped at 333,333 records.
questions.f: The query optimizer considers a custom index when a filter matches under 30% of records, capped at one million records.
questions.x: Custom indexes have the stricter 10% threshold with a 333,333-record cap. The 30% figure with a one-million cap is the starting point for standard indexes.

questions.t: Skinny tables are limited to 200 columns and are copied automatically only to Full sandboxes.
questions.f: Skinny tables are limited to 200 columns and are copied automatically to every sandbox type.
questions.x: Skinny tables are created by Salesforce Support and only Full sandboxes receive them automatically. They also can't include fields from other objects.

questions.t: To delete a million or more records, Salesforce's LDV guide recommends the hard-delete option of Bulk API or Bulk API 2.0.
questions.f: To delete a million or more records, Salesforce's LDV guide recommends a normal delete and letting the Recycle Bin empty itself.
questions.x: Soft-deleted rows stay in the Recycle Bin and still weigh on performance. Hard delete skips that, and children should be deleted before parents.

questions.t: The Hyperforce EU Operating Zone treats all 27 member states as one zone, so customers can't choose a specific EU country.
questions.f: The Hyperforce EU Operating Zone lets customers choose a specific EU member state in which to keep their data.
questions.x: The EU Operating Zone is a single region spanning the whole bloc. Its value is in-region support and contractual transfer limits, not country-level placement.

questions.t: Hyperforce Operating Zones are offered only on Hyperforce running on AWS.
questions.f: Hyperforce Operating Zones are offered only on Hyperforce running on Google Cloud.
questions.x: The Operating Zone offering runs on the AWS substrate. Hyperforce on Google Cloud is a planned footprint, not where Operating Zones run.

questions.t: The Hyperforce Switzerland Operating Zone keeps data in Switzerland but is supported by EU-based staff.
questions.f: The Hyperforce Switzerland Operating Zone keeps data in Switzerland and is supported only by staff based in Switzerland.
questions.x: The Swiss zone provides in-country storage, while support comes from personnel in the EU. Customers with Swiss-only staffing needs should take that into account.

questions.t: Under FedRAMP's 2026 relabelling, Class C corresponds to the Moderate baseline and Class D to High.
questions.f: Under FedRAMP's 2026 relabelling, Class C corresponds to the High baseline and Class D to Moderate.
questions.x: The letters rise with impact: Class B covers Low and LI-SaaS, Class C is Moderate and Class D is High. Salesforce now calls Government Cloud Plus Class D.

questions.t: If any one of confidentiality, integrity or availability is rated High under FedRAMP, the whole system must meet the High baseline.
questions.f: If one of confidentiality, integrity or availability is rated High under FedRAMP, only that objective needs High controls.
questions.x: FedRAMP baselines can't be tailored per security objective. The highest of the three FIPS 199 ratings sets the baseline for the entire system.

questions.t: Salesforce warns that AppExchange apps generally fall outside its FedRAMP authorization boundary, even if built natively on the platform.
questions.f: Salesforce states that natively built AppExchange apps automatically fall inside its FedRAMP authorization boundary.
questions.x: Authorization covers a specific offering and boundary. Installed apps, even native ones, usually aren't included and need separate review.

questions.t: An object can have two active restriction rules in Enterprise and Developer editions, and five in Performance and Unlimited.
questions.f: An object can have five active restriction rules in Enterprise and Developer editions, and ten in Performance and Unlimited.
questions.x: The per-object cap is two in Enterprise and Developer and five in Performance and Unlimited. For any one user, only one restriction or scoping rule per object should apply.

questions.t: Restriction rules don't limit users with View All Data or View All Records, who still see every record.
questions.f: Restriction rules also limit users with View All Data or View All Records, overriding those permissions.
questions.x: Broad permissions such as View All Data, View All Records and Modify All bypass restriction rules, as does code running in system mode.

questions.t: Restriction rule criteria support only the equals operator, with no AND, OR or formula logic.
questions.f: Restriction rule criteria support equals and not-equals operators combined with AND and OR logic.
questions.x: Each criterion is a single-field equality check, optionally with comma-separated values. Complex conditions usually need a helper field kept up to date by automation.

questions.t: Guest user sharing rules can grant only Read Only access to unauthenticated site visitors.
questions.f: Guest user sharing rules can grant Read Only or Read/Write access to unauthenticated site visitors.
questions.x: Guest rules are limited to Read Only. With secure guest record access on, they are the only way to share records with guests, and they expose every matching record at once.

questions.t: Per the archived Summer '20 Security Guide, an object can have 300 sharing rules, of which up to 50 may be criteria-based or guest rules.
questions.f: Per the archived Summer '20 Security Guide, an object can have 300 sharing rules, of which up to 200 may be criteria-based or guest rules.
questions.x: The guide caps the total at 300 per object with a sub-limit of 50 for criteria-based and guest user rules. Check your org's current allocations before relying on them.

questions.t: Sharing rules can only widen access; they can never make access stricter than the organization-wide default.
questions.f: Sharing rules can widen or narrow access, making it stricter than the organization-wide default for selected users.
questions.x: Sharing rules add lateral exceptions on top of a restrictive baseline. To narrow what users see, a different control such as restriction rules is needed.

questions.t: Salesforce's Apex testing guidance says bulk trigger tests should use at least 20 records.
questions.f: Salesforce's Apex testing guidance says bulk trigger tests should use at least 2,000 records.
questions.x: Testing triggers with 20 or more records exercises bulk behaviour. Good suites also cover single records, negative cases and different users via runAs.

questions.t: Well-Architected guidance maps integration testing to Partial Copy sandboxes and performance testing to Full Copy sandboxes.
questions.f: Well-Architected guidance maps integration testing to Full Copy sandboxes and performance testing to Partial Copy sandboxes.
questions.x: Partial Copy sandboxes carry representative data for integration tests, while Full Copy sandboxes mirror production for performance testing and staging. Developer sandboxes host unit testing.

questions.t: Well-Architected guidance suggests load testing quarterly at 3x to 5x current production volumes.
questions.f: Well-Architected guidance suggests load testing once a year at 10x current production volumes.
questions.x: The recommendation is a quarterly load test at three to five times today's volume, ahead of major releases. Salesforce Support should be told before performance tests run.

questions.t: Once a classic approval process has been activated, you can't add, delete or reorder its steps, even after deactivating it.
questions.f: Once a classic approval process has been activated, you can add, delete or reorder its steps as soon as you deactivate it.
questions.x: Activation permanently fixes a classic process's step structure and reject or skip behaviour; deactivating doesn't reopen it. Testing in a sandbox first avoids having to rebuild the process.

questions.t: Salesforce stopped supporting workflow rules on December 31, 2025, but existing active rules keep executing without bug fixes.
questions.f: Salesforce stopped supporting workflow rules on December 31, 2025, and existing active rules were automatically deactivated on that date.
questions.x: Since end of support, active workflow rules still run; Salesforce just no longer provides support or fixes for them. They were not switched off automatically.

questions.t: The Migrate to Flow tool converts workflow rules whose only actions are same-record field updates into fast field update (before-save) flows.
questions.f: The Migrate to Flow tool converts workflow rules whose only actions are same-record field updates into scheduled-path after-save flows.
questions.x: Rules limited to same-record field updates become before-save fast field update flows. Scheduled paths are where time-dependent actions map, not plain field updates.

questions.t: In a Field Service scheduling policy, work rules filter out ineligible candidates while service objectives rank the remaining candidates.
questions.f: In a Field Service scheduling policy, service objectives filter out ineligible candidates while work rules rank the remaining candidates.
questions.x: Work rules are pass/fail filters such as skills, availability and territory; service objectives such as minimizing travel grade the survivors. The false version swaps their roles.

questions.t: By default, Field Service appointment priority uses a 1-10 scale where 1 is the highest priority.
questions.f: By default, Field Service appointment priority uses a 1-10 scale where 10 is the highest priority.
questions.x: The optimizer's default priority scale runs 1 to 10 with 1 as most important (a 1-100 scale is optional), so treating 10 as highest inverts it.

questions.t: Field Service technicians log in to the Field Service mobile app through their org's My Domain.
questions.f: Field Service technicians log in to the Field Service mobile app through their org's Experience Cloud site.
questions.x: The mobile app for iOS and Android signs workers in via the org's My Domain; an Experience Cloud site is not the login path the article describes.

questions.t: In Marketing Cloud Engagement, an Automation Studio SQL query activity is deactivated automatically after 24 consecutive failures.
questions.f: In Marketing Cloud Engagement, an Automation Studio SQL query activity is deactivated automatically after 10 consecutive failures.
questions.x: Query activities are switched off after 24 failures in a row, not 10, so monitoring failing automations matters before they silently stop.

questions.t: Once started, a Marketing Cloud Connect synchronized data source cannot be deleted, only paused.
questions.f: Once started, a Marketing Cloud Connect synchronized data source can be deleted, but not paused.
questions.x: Synchronized data sources can only be paused after they start; deletion is not available, which is the reverse of the false claim.

questions.t: Every CRM contact or lead synchronized through Marketing Cloud Connect counts as a contact in Contact Builder, even if it is never messaged.
questions.f: Only CRM contacts or leads that are actually messaged after syncing through Marketing Cloud Connect count as contacts in Contact Builder.
questions.x: Synchronizing a record is enough for it to count as a Contact Builder contact, whether or not you ever send to it, which affects contact counts.

questions.t: In Agentforce Revenue Management, edits to pricing data take effect only after an admin runs Sync Pricing Data.
questions.f: In Agentforce Revenue Management, edits to pricing data take effect only after an admin reactivates the pricing procedure.
questions.x: Pricing changes are applied once Sync Pricing Data is run; reactivating a pricing procedure is not the step the article names.

questions.t: Salesforce CPQ is end of sale but not end of life: existing customers keep support and critical fixes, with no forced migration date.
questions.f: Salesforce CPQ is end of life with a forced migration date: existing customers keep support and critical fixes only until then.
questions.x: Salesforce stopped selling CPQ to new customers but has announced no retirement date or forced migration; existing customers still get support and critical fixes, just no new features.

questions.t: Product Configurator rules in Agentforce Revenue Management are written in Constraint Modeling Language (CML).
questions.f: Product Configurator rules in Agentforce Revenue Management are written in Salesforce Object Query Language (SOQL).
questions.x: The developer guide says configurator rules use Constraint Modeling Language; SOQL is a query language, not the rule language for the configurator.

questions.t: Each Data 360 calculated insight can have up to 10 dimensions and 50 measures.
questions.f: Each Data 360 calculated insight can have up to 50 dimensions and 10 measures.
questions.x: The limits page allows 10 dimensions and 50 measures per calculated insight; the false version swaps the two numbers.

questions.t: Data 360 streaming insights can use only Count or Sum for their measures, with up to 5 measures each.
questions.f: Data 360 streaming insights can use only Count or Average for their measures, with up to 5 measures each.
questions.x: Streaming insight measures are restricted to Count and Sum, capped at 5 per insight; Average is not one of the allowed aggregations.

questions.t: A segment-ready calculated insight must include the primary key of the object you segment on, such as Unified Individual, as a dimension.
questions.f: A segment-ready calculated insight must include only a business key, such as an order number, as a dimension.
questions.x: To be usable in segmentation, an insight has to join the segment-on object and group by its primary key; grouping by just a business key is the common mistake.

questions.t: The Data 360 Consultant prep module describes the exam as 60 questions with a 62% passing score.
questions.f: The Data 360 Consultant prep module describes the exam as 65 questions with a 68% passing score.
questions.x: Trailhead's prep module lists 60 questions and a 62% pass mark; 65 questions and 68% do not match the module.

questions.t: In the Data Cloud Consultant exam outline, data ingestion and modeling is the most heavily weighted section at 20%.
questions.f: In the Data Cloud Consultant exam outline, identity resolution is the most heavily weighted section at 20%.
questions.x: Data ingestion and modeling carries 20%, the largest weight; identity resolution is weighted at 14%.

questions.t: The Data 360 Consultant certification has no required prerequisite, though the prep module suggests earning the Salesforce Administrator credential first.
questions.f: The Data 360 Consultant certification requires the Salesforce Administrator credential as a prerequisite before candidates can register.
questions.x: No prerequisite is mandatory; holding the Administrator credential is only recommended by the prep module.

questions.t: Data 360 data model object API names end in __dlm, while data lake object API names end in __dlo.
questions.f: Data 360 data model object API names end in __dlo, while data lake object API names end in __dlm.
questions.x: DMOs use the __dlm suffix and DLOs use __dlo; the false version swaps them. DMO fields themselves end in __c.

questions.t: A custom data model object created from a data lake object is not linked to the rest of the data model automatically, so you define its relationships.
questions.f: A custom data model object created from a data lake object inherits the relationships of the standard model automatically, so none need defining.
questions.x: Custom DMOs take the DLO's label and API name but no relationships; you must add them yourself between DMOs.

questions.t: In Data 360, contact details such as email addresses belong on Contact Point data model objects rather than on the Individual object.
questions.f: In Data 360, contact details such as email addresses belong on the Individual data model object rather than on Contact Point objects.
questions.x: Trailhead's modeling guidance puts emails, phones and addresses on Contact Point Email, Phone and Address DMOs, keeping Individual free of contact details.

questions.t: A source record joins a unified profile if it meets any one match rule in the ruleset, but it must satisfy every criterion within that rule.
questions.f: A source record joins a unified profile only if it meets every match rule in the ruleset, but it needs to satisfy just one criterion within each rule.
questions.x: Match rules are ORed while the criteria inside a rule are ANDed. That is why adding rules raises the consolidation rate and adding criteria to a rule lowers it; the false statement reverses both.

questions.t: An identity resolution ruleset ID can be at most four characters long and cannot be changed after it is set.
questions.f: An identity resolution ruleset ID can be up to forty characters long and can be renamed at any time after it is set.
questions.x: The Trailhead module describes the optional ruleset ID as limited to four characters and fixed once saved. Both the forty-character length and the ability to rename it are wrong.

questions.t: Real-time identity resolution for Web and Mobile SDK data runs in milliseconds but treats fuzzy match criteria as exact.
questions.f: Real-time identity resolution for Web and Mobile SDK data runs in milliseconds and applies fuzzy match criteria exactly as batch resolution does.
questions.x: Real-time matching trades fuzziness for speed: fuzzy criteria are evaluated as exact, with phone and email using Exact Normalized. Batch resolution is where fuzzy methods behave as configured.

questions.t: To give record types different Opportunity Stage values, you assign each record type a different sales process.
questions.f: To give record types different Opportunity Stage values, you trim the Stage picklist directly on each record type.
questions.x: Opportunity Stage, Case and Solution Status and Lead Status are reserved: their values come from a business process, not record type picklist trimming. So you vary them by assigning a different process to each record type.

questions.t: Salesforce recommends keeping an org at no more than 200 record types, because beyond that they become hard to manage.
questions.f: Salesforce recommends keeping an org at no more than 20 record types, because beyond that they become hard to manage.
questions.x: The record type limitations guidance puts the recommended ceiling at 200. Twenty understates it by a factor of ten.

questions.t: Apex describe methods such as getRecordTypeInfosByDeveloperName() return record types even when the running user has no access to them.
questions.f: Apex describe methods such as getRecordTypeInfosByDeveloperName() return only the record types the running user has access to.
questions.x: DescribeSObjectResult lists every record type regardless of the user's access. To honour access in a custom UI, check isAvailable() on each RecordTypeInfo instead of relying on the describe result being filtered.

questions.t: An org can have 5 batch jobs queued or active at once, and up to 100 more can wait in Holding status in the Apex flex queue.
questions.f: An org can have 25 batch jobs queued or active at once, and up to 1,000 more can wait in Holding status in the Apex flex queue.
questions.x: Batch Apex allows five queued or active jobs per org plus 100 held in the flex queue; once that queue is full, executeBatch throws a LimitException. The 25 and 1,000 figures are invented.

questions.t: In a batch class that implements Database.Stateful, instance variables keep their values across chunks, while static variables still reset.
questions.f: In a batch class that implements Database.Stateful, static variables keep their values across chunks, while instance variables still reset.
questions.x: Database.Stateful preserves instance member variables between execute calls, which is how running totals are kept. Static variables are reset for each chunk either way, so the false statement swaps the two.

questions.t: A batch class that implements Database.RaisesPlatformEvents publishes a BatchApexErrorEvent when start, execute or finish hits an unhandled exception.
questions.f: A batch class that implements Database.AllowsCallouts publishes a BatchApexErrorEvent when start, execute or finish hits an unhandled exception.
questions.x: Database.RaisesPlatformEvents is the opt-in for BatchApexErrorEvent, which carries the job ID, failed scope record IDs and exception details. Database.AllowsCallouts only permits HTTP callouts from the batch.

questions.t: Lightning Web Security is the default for orgs created in Winter '23 or later; older orgs default to Lightning Locker unless LWS is enabled.
questions.f: Lightning Web Security is the default for orgs created in Winter '20 or later; older orgs default to Lightning Locker unless LWS is enabled.
questions.x: LWS became the default for orgs created from Winter '23 and has been GA for LWC and Aura in all orgs since Summer '23. Winter '20 predates that change, so the false statement gets the release wrong.

questions.t: In Lightning Web Components, records are read with @wire adapters such as getRecord, while createRecord and updateRecord are called as promise-based functions.
questions.f: In Lightning Web Components, records are read with @wire adapters such as getRecord, and createRecord and updateRecord are also wired with @wire.
questions.x: LDS reads use wire adapters from the lightning/ui*Api modules, but writes use imperative, promise-returning functions. Wiring is only for reads, so createRecord and updateRecord cannot be wired.

questions.t: An Apex method that queries Task or Event must be called imperatively from a Lightning web component, because UI API doesn't support those objects.
questions.f: An Apex method that queries Task or Event must be wired with @wire in a Lightning web component, because UI API doesn't support those objects.
questions.x: Only non-mutating @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) methods can be wired; methods touching objects UI API lacks, such as Task and Event, must be called imperatively and return a promise.

questions.t: In Salesforce Code Analyzer, the --rule-selector flag defaults to Recommended when you run sf code-analyzer run without it.
questions.f: In Salesforce Code Analyzer, the --rule-selector flag defaults to all rules when you run sf code-analyzer run without it.
questions.x: The run command uses the Recommended selector unless you choose engines, severities, names or tags yourself. It does not run every one of the 500-plus built-in rules by default.

questions.t: Code Analyzer's --severity-threshold flag sets the lowest severity that makes the command exit non-zero, which lets a CI pipeline fail the build.
questions.f: Code Analyzer's --severity-threshold flag sets the lowest severity that is written to the output file, which filters what reviewers see.
questions.x: The threshold controls the exit code: any finding at or above it produces a non-zero exit so the pipeline fails. It is not an output filter; output files are controlled by --output-file.

questions.t: Code Analyzer v5 added the Flow Scanner engine, which audits Flows for security issues.
questions.f: Code Analyzer v5 added the RetireJS engine, which audits Flows for security issues.
questions.x: Flow Scanner, along with Regex, was new in v5 and is the engine that checks Flows. RetireJS instead checks third-party JavaScript libraries for known vulnerabilities.

questions.t: Composite Batch is not transactional: each successful subrequest commits at once and isn't rolled back if a later subrequest fails.
questions.f: Composite Batch is fully transactional: all subrequests commit together and are rolled back if a later subrequest fails.
questions.x: Composite Batch runs up to 25 independent subrequests serially with no shared transaction, so earlier successes stay committed. Use sObject Tree or Composite with allOrNone when you need rollback.

questions.t: An sObject Tree request can create up to 200 records in total, across no more than five object types and trees at most five levels deep.
questions.f: An sObject Tree request can create up to 2,000 records in total, across no more than ten object types and trees at most ten levels deep.
questions.x: sObject Tree is capped at 200 records, five object types and five levels per request, and it is all-or-nothing. The 2,000 and ten figures are inflated.

questions.t: In sObject Collections, allOrNone defaults to false, so each record succeeds or fails independently unless rollback is requested.
questions.f: In sObject Collections, allOrNone defaults to true, so a single failed record rolls back the whole request unless partial success is requested.
questions.x: sObject Collections processes records independently by default and still returns HTTP 200 when some fail, so clients must check each result's success flag. Rollback only happens if allOrNone is set to true.

questions.t: Salesforce's decision guide notes that platform events and Change Data Capture both have a 3-day replay period and a 1 MB message limit.
questions.f: Salesforce's decision guide notes that platform events and Change Data Capture both have a 7-day replay period and a 10 MB message limit.
questions.x: The event-driven decision guide gives both mechanisms a three-day replay window and a 1 MB cap per message. Seven days and 10 MB overstate both limits.

questions.t: An event relay that sends event bus messages to Amazon EventBridge is created in a stopped state and is started after the partner event source is activated.
questions.f: An event relay that sends event bus messages to Amazon EventBridge is created in a running state and starts before the partner event source is activated.
questions.x: A new event relay begins stopped; you activate the partner event source in EventBridge first and then start the relay. It does not begin running on creation.

questions.t: In the fanout event pattern, all subscribers read the same message from a single queue, which makes it harder to confirm a given subscriber received it.
questions.f: In the fanout event pattern, each subscriber receives its own unique copy of the message, which makes it easy to confirm a given subscriber received it.
questions.x: Fanout shares one queued message among all subscribers, which is efficient for mass notifications but weak on per-subscriber confirmation. A unique copy per subscriber describes the publish/subscribe pattern instead.

questions.t: If an outbound message's endpoint is unreachable, Salesforce retries with gaps capped at two hours and drops messages older than 24 hours.
questions.f: If an outbound message's endpoint is unreachable, Salesforce retries with gaps capped at two hours and drops messages older than 72 hours.
questions.x: Outbound messaging retries with exponential backoff (at most two hours apart) but gives up once a message is 24 hours old. The 72-hour figure is the replay window of platform events and CDC, not outbound messaging.

questions.t: One outbound messaging SOAP call can carry up to 100 notifications, and the listener replies with a single Ack that covers all of them.
questions.f: One outbound messaging SOAP call can carry up to 100 notifications, and the listener must reply with a separate Ack for each notification.
questions.x: The WSDL's notifications() call batches up to 100 notifications, and the listener returns one boolean Ack for the whole message. There is no per-notification acknowledgement.

questions.t: With Send Session ID enabled, an outbound message carries a session for the definition's User to send as, not for the user who changed the record.
questions.f: With Send Session ID enabled, an outbound message carries a session for the user who changed the record, not for the definition's User to send as.
questions.x: The session included for callbacks belongs to the User to send as configured on the outbound message, whose permissions also govern what data is sent. The user whose edit fired the message is not the session owner.

questions.t: Under the DoD Cloud Computing SRG, a FedRAMP Moderate or High authorization is treated as essentially sufficient for Impact Level 2.
questions.f: Under the DoD Cloud Computing SRG, a FedRAMP Moderate or High authorization is treated as essentially sufficient for Impact Level 4.
questions.x: At IL2 DoD reuses the FedRAMP Moderate or High authorization with no extra NIST control assessments. Higher levels such as IL4 add FedRAMP+ controls and parameter values on top.

questions.t: A DoD Provisional Authorization under the Cloud Computing SRG attaches to a specific cloud service offering rather than to the provider as a whole.
questions.f: A DoD Provisional Authorization under the Cloud Computing SRG attaches to the cloud provider as a whole rather than to a specific service offering.
questions.x: The DISA authorizing official grants each PA for one cloud service offering, so a provider's other offerings are not covered. That is why Salesforce's PAs apply only to the Government Cloud Plus environments.

questions.t: The first DoD Cloud Computing SRG collapsed the Cloud Security Model's six levels into four, keeping the numbers 2, 4, 5 and 6.
questions.f: The first DoD Cloud Computing SRG collapsed the Cloud Security Model's six levels into four, keeping the numbers 1, 3, 5 and 6.
questions.x: Old levels 1 and 3 were folded into the next level up, so the surviving impact levels are numbered 2, 4, 5 and 6. Levels 1 and 3 no longer exist.

questions.t: If any single FIPS 199 security objective, such as integrity, is rated High, FedRAMP requires the entire cloud offering to meet the High baseline.
questions.f: If any single FIPS 199 security objective, such as integrity, is rated High, FedRAMP requires only that objective's controls to meet the High baseline.
questions.x: FedRAMP does not allow tailoring by security objective, so one High objective lifts the whole offering to High. Applying High controls to just that objective is exactly the tailoring FedRAMP disallows.

questions.t: In its draft Rev. 5 baselines, FedRAMP added 22 controls above the NIST high baseline for High, versus 17 above the moderate baseline for Moderate.
questions.f: In its draft Rev. 5 baselines, FedRAMP added 17 controls above the NIST high baseline for High, versus 22 above the moderate baseline for Moderate.
questions.x: The December 2021 draft added 22 FedRAMP-specific controls to High, 17 to Moderate and 1 to Low. The false version swaps the High and Moderate counts.

questions.t: Federal agencies request Salesforce's FedRAMP High package through the FedRAMP PMO, while state and local bodies go through their Salesforce account executive.
questions.f: Federal agencies request Salesforce's FedRAMP High package through their Salesforce account executive, while state and local bodies go through the FedRAMP PMO.
questions.x: The FedRAMP PMO handles requests from .gov or .mil addresses, so federal agencies use that route. State, local and partner organizations instead ask their Salesforce account executive.

questions.t: The Revised 508 Standards incorporate WCAG 2.0 by reference, requiring its Level A and Level AA success criteria.
questions.f: The Revised 508 Standards incorporate WCAG 2.0 by reference, requiring its Level A, Level AA and Level AAA success criteria.
questions.x: Section 508's technical rules point to WCAG 2.0 and require conformance at Levels A and AA. Level AAA is not part of the requirement.

questions.t: Salesforce's posted Accessibility Conformance Reports are contractual only when the contract explicitly includes them or an equivalent.
questions.f: Salesforce's posted Accessibility Conformance Reports are contractual for every customer once they are published for a product release.
questions.x: Publishing an ACR does not make it a commitment; an agency that wants one must negotiate it into the contract. Treating posted reports as automatically binding is a common procurement mistake.

questions.t: On a Lightning page, a right-sidebar template gives keyboard users a shorter path to the main content than a left-sidebar template.
questions.f: On a Lightning page, a left-sidebar template gives keyboard users a shorter path to the main content than a right-sidebar template.
questions.x: With a left sidebar, tab order runs through the sidebar before reaching the main content, which lengthens keyboard navigation. A right sidebar puts the main content earlier in the tab order.

questions.t: Each custom object can have up to 10 Apex sharing reasons, and deleting a reason deletes all sharing on the object that uses it.
questions.f: Each custom object can have up to 25 Apex sharing reasons, and deleting a reason deletes all sharing on the object that uses it.
questions.x: The limit is 10 Apex sharing reasons per custom object, not 25. Because deleting a reason also deletes every share row using it, reasons should be removed with care.

questions.t: A share row inserted from Apex without a custom sharing reason gets the Manual row cause and is removed when the record owner changes.
questions.f: A share row inserted from Apex without a custom sharing reason gets an Apex row cause and is kept when the record owner changes.
questions.x: Without an Apex sharing reason, code-inserted shares default to the Manual cause and behave like user-managed sharing, which ownership changes wipe out. Only rows with a custom reason survive owner changes.

questions.t: Creating an Apex sharing reason requires the Author Apex permission, while adding or changing shares that use a reason requires Modify All Data.
questions.f: Creating an Apex sharing reason requires the Modify All Data permission, while adding or changing shares that use a reason requires Author Apex.
questions.x: Defining the reason is an Author Apex task, whereas managing the reason-based share rows themselves needs Modify All Data. The false statement swaps the two permissions.

questions.t: A new Sales Territories model starts in the Planning state, which grants no record access until the model is activated.
questions.f: A new Sales Territories model starts in the Active state, which grants record access to territory members as soon as it is saved.
questions.x: Planning is the default state for a new model and lets admins build and preview it without affecting access. Users get territory-based access only after the model is activated.

questions.t: An opportunity gets at most one territory, chosen by an Apex class that implements the OpportunityTerritory2AssignmentFilter interface.
questions.f: An opportunity gets up to three territories, chosen by an Apex class that implements the OpportunityTerritory2AssignmentFilter interface.
questions.x: Accounts can sit in several territories, but an opportunity is limited to one. The filter class picks it from the parent account's territories, using priority or custom logic when there are several.

questions.t: The Sales Territories implementation guide allows up to four territory models per org including clones, or two in Enterprise Edition.
questions.f: The Sales Territories implementation guide allows up to ten territory models per org including clones, or four in Enterprise Edition.
questions.x: The guide gives four models per org (two in Enterprise Edition), clones counted, with only one active at a time. Ten and four overstate those figures.

questions.t: Implicit sharing covers standard objects only; custom objects fall outside it and need other mechanisms to open record access.
questions.f: Implicit sharing covers standard and custom objects alike, so custom objects need no other mechanism to open record access.
questions.x: Salesforce's sharing guidance flags that implicit sharing does not reach custom objects, an edge case scenario questions hinge on. Assuming custom objects inherit implicit parent or child access is the mistake in the false version.

questions.t: Because of sharing recalculation cost, Salesforce guidance suggests keeping structural hierarchy changes to roughly once a quarter.
questions.f: Because of sharing recalculation cost, Salesforce guidance suggests keeping structural hierarchy changes to roughly once a week.
questions.x: Each structural hierarchy change triggers sharing recalculation, so the guidance treats it as a design constraint and suggests about quarterly changes. Weekly restructuring would cause far more recalculation than recommended.

questions.t: On the Defer Sharing Calculations page, suspending group membership calculation also suspends sharing rule calculation.
questions.f: On the Defer Sharing Calculations page, suspending group membership calculation leaves sharing rule calculation running.
questions.x: Pausing group membership calculation pauses sharing rule calculation along with it, and resuming group membership then calls for a full sharing rule recalculation. The two engines cannot be split that way, so sharing rules do not keep calculating on their own.

questions.t: The Defer Sharing Calculations permission is off by default, and an org gets it by contacting Salesforce.
questions.f: The Defer Sharing Calculations permission is off by default, and an admin turns it on under Sharing Settings in Setup.
questions.x: Deferring sharing calculations is not self-service: the permission starts disabled and Salesforce enables it on request. An admin cannot switch it on from Sharing Settings.

questions.t: Apex sharing recalculation classes can be associated only with custom objects, whose org-wide default must not already be Public Read/Write.
questions.f: Apex sharing recalculation classes can be associated with standard or custom objects, whose org-wide default must not already be Public Read/Write.
questions.x: The Apex Sharing Recalculations setting exists only for custom objects that use Apex managed sharing. Standard objects cannot have a recalculation class attached.

questions.t: To qualify for the CTA review board, a candidate must already hold both the System Architect and the Application Architect credentials.
questions.f: To qualify for the CTA review board, a candidate must already hold either the System Architect or the Application Architect credential.
questions.x: Eligibility for the CTA board requires both architect credentials, each earned by stacking domain architect certifications. Holding only one of them is not enough to register.

questions.t: The Architect Review Board Evaluation is delivered online only, while the Technical Architect Review Board Exam can be taken online or in person.
questions.f: The Architect Review Board Evaluation can be taken online or in person, while the Technical Architect Review Board Exam is delivered online only.
questions.x: Trailhead lists the evaluation step as online only and the full exam as available online or in person. The false version swaps the delivery options of the two steps.

questions.t: Since 2023, CTA review board diagrams must be produced digitally with designated tools, and hand-drawn diagrams are no longer accepted.
questions.f: Since 2023, CTA review board diagrams may be produced digitally with designated tools or drawn by hand on flip charts.
questions.x: In 2023 Salesforce moved the board to digital artifacts built in designated tools and stopped accepting hand-drawn diagrams. Hand-drawn work is therefore no longer an option.

questions.t: The Salesforce Diagrams framework on the Architecture Center defines six diagram types, including capability map, system landscape and data model.
questions.f: The Salesforce Diagrams framework on the Architecture Center defines four diagram types, including capability map, system landscape and data model.
questions.x: The framework has six types: capability map, system landscape, solution architecture, roadmap, interaction/process/flow, and data model. Four undercounts it.

questions.t: The Architecture Center's diagram templates are built for Lucidchart, and footer icons in template-based diagrams can become detached from their cards.
questions.f: The Architecture Center's diagram templates are built for Microsoft Visio, and footer icons in template-based diagrams can become detached from their cards.
questions.x: Salesforce provides its diagram templates for Lucidchart and warns that footer icons may come loose from their cards. Visio is not the target tool for these templates.

questions.t: When the Architecture Center launched in beta in December 2020, it organized resources by four modes of architect work: design, deliver, govern and roadmap.
questions.f: When the Architecture Center launched in beta in December 2020, it organized resources by the five Well-Architected pillars, from Trust to Fairness.
questions.x: The original beta site grouped content by the design, deliver, govern and roadmap modes of architect work. The five-pillar Well-Architected structure is much later, shown on the site as of Winter '27.

questions.t: In ATAM, a tradeoff point is a design element that several quality attributes are sensitive to at once, so tuning it helps one quality and hurts another.
questions.f: In ATAM, a tradeoff point is a design element where a change noticeably moves a single quality attribute without affecting the others.
questions.x: ATAM calls an element that moves one attribute a sensitivity point; a tradeoff point is one several attributes depend on simultaneously. The false statement describes a sensitivity point, not a tradeoff point.

questions.t: The record-triggered automation decision guide points to an Apex trigger framework when an object has more than 30 automations or 5+ downstream DML.
questions.f: The record-triggered automation decision guide points to a hybrid of Flow plus invocable Apex when an object has more than 30 automations or 5+ downstream DML.
questions.x: The hybrid Flow plus invocable Apex approach is the guide's middle band of 15 to 30 automations with 2 to 4 downstream DML. Beyond 30 automations or at 5+ downstream DML, the guide recommends an Apex trigger framework.

questions.t: The record-triggered automation decision guide advises one automation entry point per object, since mixing flows and triggers on it makes ordering unpredictable.
questions.f: The record-triggered automation decision guide advises mixing flows and triggers on each object, since splitting the logic makes ordering more predictable.
questions.x: Combining flows and triggers on the same object fragments ownership and makes execution order hard to predict, so the guide recommends a single entry point. The false statement reverses that advice.

questions.t: In a record-triggered flow, adding a fault path to a failing element lets the triggering record change still complete even though the flow failed.
questions.f: In a record-triggered flow, adding a fault path to a failing element still blocks the triggering record change and shows the error to the user.
questions.x: A fault path marks the error as handled, so the triggering save goes through and earlier work is not undone automatically. Blocking the save with a message is what happens with no fault path, or when the path ends in a Custom Error element.

questions.t: Each Update Records action in a Process Builder process costs one SOQL query plus one DML statement against the transaction's governor limits.
questions.f: Each Update Records action in a Process Builder process costs one DML statement only, with no SOQL query counted against the transaction's governor limits.
questions.x: Process limits count an Update Records action as both a query and a DML statement, while Create a Record or a quick action costs one DML statement. The false version drops the query and so understates the cost.

questions.t: Event processes in Process Builder evaluate platform event messages in replay-ID order, in batches of up to 2,000 messages, in their own transaction.
questions.f: Event processes in Process Builder evaluate platform event messages in replay-ID order, in batches of up to 200 messages, in their own transaction.
questions.x: Event-triggered processes take platform event messages asynchronously in batches as large as 2,000. The 200 figure understates the batch size.

questions.t: The Migrate to Flow tool converts record change processes, but it does not convert event or invocable processes or processes that have scheduled actions.
questions.f: The Migrate to Flow tool converts record change, event and invocable processes, including processes that have scheduled actions.
questions.x: Only record change processes with supported actions are converted; event processes, invocable processes and anything with scheduled actions or field traversals must be rebuilt by hand. The false version claims the tool covers every process type.

questions.t: In the Slack Platform, messages, modals and canvases are available to every kind of app, while the App Home tab is limited to apps built with Bolt.
questions.f: In the Slack Platform, messages, App Home and canvases are available to every kind of app, while modals are limited to apps built with Bolt.
questions.x: Slack opens messages, modals and canvases to all apps but reserves the App Home surface for Bolt apps. The false version swaps App Home and modals.

questions.t: The Slack Events API delivers at most 30,000 events per workspace per app per 60 minutes, then sends an app_rate_limited event.
questions.f: The Slack Events API delivers at most 3,000 events per workspace per app per 60 minutes, then sends an app_rate_limited event.
questions.x: The Events API ceiling is 30,000 events per workspace per app each hour; past that Slack signals app_rate_limited. The false figure is ten times too low.

questions.t: The Apex SDK for Slack, which lets Apex define Slack apps and handle their events, is still labelled Beta in Salesforce documentation.
questions.f: The Apex SDK for Slack, which lets Apex define Slack apps and handle their events, is labelled generally available in Salesforce documentation.
questions.x: Salesforce marks the Apex SDK for Slack as Beta, so it can be discontinued without notice and production designs carry that risk. Describing it as GA is wrong.

questions.t: A time trigger can be added to a workflow rule only while the rule is inactive and has no pending actions in the time-based queue.
questions.f: A time trigger can be added to a workflow rule only while the rule is active and has no pending actions in the time-based queue.
questions.x: Salesforce requires the rule to be deactivated, with nothing queued and without the create-and-every-edit evaluation setting, before a time trigger can be added. The false version wrongly says the rule must be active.

questions.t: On Tableau Cloud, multi-factor authentication is required for all users.
questions.f: On Tableau Cloud, multi-factor authentication is required only for site administrators.
questions.x: Tableau Cloud enforces MFA for every user, not just admins. Because Cloud also lacks direct Active Directory, LDAP and Kerberos sign-in, identity is integrated through SAML or OIDC.

questions.t: Tableau Next is licensed separately, as Creator or Consumer, rather than through the Viewer, Explorer and Creator licenses of Tableau by Tableau.
questions.f: Tableau Next is licensed through the same Viewer, Explorer and Creator licenses used by Tableau Cloud and Tableau Server.
questions.x: Tableau Next and the original Tableau portfolio are separate products with separate licenses. Tableau Next uses Creator and Consumer licenses; Viewer, Explorer and Creator belong to Tableau by Tableau.

questions.t: The Tableau+ bundle, which adds Data 360 credits and Tableau Next to user licenses, is offered only for Tableau Cloud.
questions.f: The Tableau+ bundle, which adds Data 360 credits and Tableau Next to user licenses, is offered for both Tableau Cloud and Tableau Server.
questions.x: Tableau+ is a Cloud-only bundle. Self-managed Tableau Server customers can't buy it, so the bundle presumes the hosted deployment.

questions.t: Zero copy file federation reads external files with Data 360's own compute, so it avoids the warehouse's compute fees.
questions.f: Zero copy query federation reads external files with Data 360's own compute, so it avoids the warehouse's compute fees.
questions.x: File federation bypasses the external warehouse's compute layer and reads storage directly. Query federation sends queries to the external engine over JDBC, so it can incur that platform's compute charges.

questions.t: Under zero copy query federation, change-triggered features such as data actions work only when caching is enabled.
questions.f: Under zero copy file federation, change-triggered features such as data actions work only when caching is enabled.
questions.x: Query federation can't see changes in the external system unless caching is on. File federation can detect external changes without caching, so it doesn't carry that restriction.

questions.t: A federated external data lake object, and any DMO mapped to one, cannot be included in a zero copy data share.
questions.f: A federated external data lake object can be included in a zero copy data share, though a DMO mapped to one cannot.
questions.x: Federated data can't be re-shared out of Data 360: both the external DLO and DMOs mapped to it are excluded from zero copy data shares.

questions.t: A custom big object's index can contain at most five custom fields, and their text fields may total no more than 100 characters.
questions.f: A custom big object's index can contain at most ten custom fields, and their text fields may total no more than 255 characters.
questions.x: The big object index, which serves as its composite primary key, takes one to five required custom fields with text fields capped at 100 characters combined. Ten fields and 255 characters overstate both limits.

questions.t: Inserting a big object record whose index values already exist overwrites the existing record instead of creating a duplicate.
questions.f: Inserting a big object record whose index values already exist fails with a duplicate error instead of overwriting the record.
questions.x: Big object writes are idempotent on the index: a matching index overwrites the stored record. That is why a failed load can simply be retried.

questions.t: In a SOQL query on a big object, range operators are allowed only on the last index field being filtered.
questions.f: In a SOQL query on a big object, range operators are allowed only on the first index field being filtered.
questions.x: Big object queries must filter index fields in order from the first, with = or IN on each, and only the last filtered field may use a range operator.

questions.t: By default an object can have up to 25 external ID fields; raising that requires a Salesforce Support case.
questions.f: By default an object can have up to 100 external ID fields; raising that requires a Salesforce Support case.
questions.x: The default allocation is 25 external IDs per object. Because each one is indexed, they also draw on the shared default of 25 custom indexes per object, so 100 is far too high.

questions.t: Upserting on a non-unique external ID field requires the View All Data permission, while a unique external ID needs no special permission.
questions.f: Upserting on a unique external ID field requires the View All Data permission, while a non-unique external ID needs no special permission.
questions.x: The extra permission applies to the non-unique case, where Salesforce must see all potential matches. Marking the external ID Unique avoids both this requirement and multiple-match errors.

questions.t: A REST upsert by external ID whose value matches more than one record returns HTTP 300 with the list of candidate records.
questions.f: A REST upsert by external ID whose value matches more than one record updates the most recently modified of those records.
questions.x: Upsert never guesses between several matches: the REST API answers 300 and lists the candidates. Zero matches insert (201) and exactly one match updates (200).

questions.t: External object API names end in __x, marking records that live in an external system rather than in the org.
questions.f: External object API names end in __e, marking records that live in an external system rather than in the org.
questions.x: External objects use the __x suffix. They are defined against an external data source and fetched on demand rather than stored in Salesforce.

questions.t: An indirect lookup links a child external object to a parent standard or custom object by matching a unique external ID field on the parent.
questions.f: An indirect lookup links a child external object to a parent standard or custom object by matching the parent's 18-character Salesforce record ID.
questions.x: External records rarely hold Salesforce IDs, so an indirect lookup matches a remote column against a unique external ID field on the parent record instead.

questions.t: For Salesforce Connect OData adapters, the result set of a single OData query is limited to 16 MB.
questions.f: For Salesforce Connect OData adapters, the result set of a single OData query is limited to 1 MB.
questions.x: Salesforce documents a 16 MB result-set limit per OData query, alongside an 8 MB limit on individual HTTP requests and responses. 1 MB understates it.

questions.t: A single Apex transaction can make at most 100 callouts, counting both HTTP requests and API calls.
questions.f: A single Apex transaction can make at most 10 callouts, counting both HTTP requests and API calls.
questions.x: The per-transaction callout limit is 100. Ten is far below the documented cap, though the 120-second cumulative timeout can still constrain many slow calls.

questions.t: An Apex callout times out after 10 seconds by default unless the code sets a custom timeout.
questions.f: An Apex callout times out after 60 seconds by default unless the code sets a custom timeout.
questions.x: The default callout timeout is 10 seconds. Code can raise it as high as 120,000 milliseconds, but 60 seconds is not the default.

questions.t: Within one Apex transaction, a callout may run before DML, but it cannot run after uncommitted DML is pending.
questions.f: Within one Apex transaction, a callout may run after DML, but it cannot run before any DML has been performed.
questions.x: Pending work such as uncommitted DML blocks a later callout, so the usual design is callout first and DML afterwards, or moving the callout into asynchronous Apex.

questions.t: Custom metadata type records deploy with packages and change sets, whereas custom settings deploy only their definitions.
questions.f: Custom settings records deploy with packages and change sets, whereas custom metadata types deploy only their definitions.
questions.x: Because custom metadata records are themselves metadata, they travel with the app. Custom settings and custom objects move only their structure, and their records must be loaded separately.

questions.t: Apex can create, read and update custom metadata records, but it cannot delete them.
questions.f: Apex can create, read and delete custom metadata records, but it cannot update them.
questions.x: Apex modifies custom metadata through the Metadata namespace, which supports create and update but not delete. That missing delete is one reason custom settings still suit full CRUD needs.

questions.t: Custom metadata usage is counted by each field's maximum size, so a nearly empty text area still uses 255 characters per record.
questions.f: Custom metadata usage is counted by the characters actually stored, so a nearly empty text area uses only the characters it holds.
questions.x: The 10-million-character allotment is consumed by field size, not content. Picklists and checkboxes count as 10 characters regardless of value.

questions.t: A Queueable duplicate signature blocks a new enqueue only while a matching job is still waiting, so a copy can be enqueued once the first starts running.
questions.f: A Queueable duplicate signature blocks a new enqueue until the matching job finishes, so no copy can be enqueued while the first is running.
questions.x: The signature is dropped when the job is dequeued, so the feature guarantees at least one run per signature rather than mutual exclusion. A second copy can be queued while the first executes.

questions.t: A Transaction Finalizer can re-enqueue a failed Queueable job up to five consecutive times.
questions.f: A Transaction Finalizer can re-enqueue a failed Queueable job up to ten consecutive times.
questions.x: Finalizers run after the job ends, including after an unhandled exception, and may re-enqueue the job after failures, but only five consecutive times, not ten.

questions.t: Queueable chains stop at a depth of five in Developer Edition and Trial orgs, while production orgs have no chain-depth cap.
questions.f: Queueable chains stop at a depth of five in production orgs, while Developer Edition and Trial orgs have no chain-depth cap.
questions.x: Chain depth is uncapped in production; the five-job limit, counting the parent, applies to Developer Edition and Trial orgs unless stack depth is configured.

questions.t: In Salesforce's pattern mapping, asynchronous inbound data integration into Salesforce is handled by the Batch Data Synchronization pattern.
questions.f: In Salesforce's pattern mapping, asynchronous inbound data integration into Salesforce is handled by the Remote Call-In pattern.
questions.x: Inbound data integration splits by timing: the asynchronous case is Batch Data Synchronization, while Remote Call-In is the synchronous inbound case.

questions.t: Salesforce's data integration decision guide states that Salesforce-to-Salesforce has reached end of life for org-to-org integration.
questions.f: Salesforce's data integration decision guide recommends Salesforce-to-Salesforce as the default tool for org-to-org integration.
questions.x: Salesforce-to-Salesforce is end of life. For org-to-org work the guide points instead to options such as Heroku Connect, MuleSoft, the native APIs, Change Data Capture or the cross-org adapter.

questions.t: Salesforce's data integration guide recommends an API Only integration user with External Client Applications rather than connected apps.
questions.f: Salesforce's data integration guide recommends a standard licensed user with connected apps rather than External Client Applications.
questions.x: For authentication the guide favours a dedicated API Only integration user and External Client Applications, steering away from connected apps and SOAP login.

questions.t: In Salesforce's integration pattern catalogue, Remote Call-In can be either synchronous or asynchronous.
questions.f: In Salesforce's integration pattern catalogue, Remote Call-In is always asynchronous.
questions.x: Request and Reply and Data Virtualization are synchronous, and Fire and Forget, Batch Data Synchronization and UI updates are asynchronous; Remote Call-In is the one pattern that can be either.

questions.t: Salesforce's integration guidance notes that platform events are published without Salesforce-side retry and can't be rolled back with the transaction.
questions.f: Salesforce's integration guidance notes that platform events are retried by Salesforce on failure and are rolled back with the transaction.
questions.x: Publishing a platform event is not tied to the transaction's rollback and Salesforce doesn't retry it, which is why designs must handle delivery and idempotency themselves.

questions.t: For someone who mainly builds MuleSoft APIs, the MuleSoft Platform Integration Architect credential is a closer fit than Platform Integration Architect.
questions.f: For someone who mainly builds MuleSoft APIs, Platform Integration Architect is a closer fit than the MuleSoft Platform Integration Architect credential.
questions.x: Platform Integration Architect focuses on designing the Salesforce side of integrations. Work centred on building MuleSoft APIs maps better to the separate MuleSoft credential.

questions.t: Salesforce's integration patterns guide states that a single Composite API call can bundle up to 25 subrequests.
questions.f: Salesforce's integration patterns guide states that a single Composite API call can bundle up to 100 subrequests.
questions.x: The guide cites 25 subrequests per Composite API call as one of its volume considerations. 100 overstates the limit.

questions.t: For the Remote Call-In pattern, Salesforce rates SOAP API and custom Apex web services as suboptimal compared with REST, Composite and Bulk API 2.0.
questions.f: For the Remote Call-In pattern, Salesforce rates SOAP API and custom Apex web services as the best fit, ahead of REST, Composite and Bulk API 2.0.
questions.x: The guide's fit ratings for Remote Call-In put the Composite, REST, Bulk API 2.0, GraphQL and Pub/Sub APIs at best, and SOAP API and custom Apex web services at suboptimal.

questions.t: For the Fire and Forget pattern, Salesforce rates outbound messaging as suboptimal, behind Flow-driven platform events and Change Data Capture.
questions.f: For the Fire and Forget pattern, Salesforce rates outbound messaging as the best fit, ahead of Flow-driven platform events and Change Data Capture.
questions.x: In the Fire and Forget ratings, platform events, Pub/Sub API and Change Data Capture are best, while outbound messaging and trigger-driven asynchronous callouts are suboptimal.

questions.t: CloudHub 2.0 is a managed, containerized iPaaS that MuleSoft operates across 12 global regions.
questions.f: CloudHub 2.0 is a managed, containerized iPaaS that MuleSoft operates across 4 global regions.
questions.x: MuleSoft runs CloudHub 2.0 in 12 regions worldwide. Four regions understates its footprint.

questions.t: Anypoint Runtime Fabric is a container service that the customer runs in its own data center or in AWS or Azure.
questions.f: Anypoint Runtime Fabric is a container service that MuleSoft operates for the customer across its global cloud regions.
questions.x: Runtime Fabric is customer-operated infrastructure on premises or in AWS or Azure. The MuleSoft-operated managed option is CloudHub, not Runtime Fabric.

questions.t: In API-led connectivity, Process APIs combine and transform data from System APIs to carry business logic.
questions.f: In API-led connectivity, Experience APIs combine and transform data from System APIs to carry business logic.
questions.x: Process APIs hold the business logic that combines System API data. Experience APIs shape that data for a particular consumer such as a mobile app.

questions.t: Calling the REST API Limits resource requires the View Setup and Configuration permission.
questions.f: Calling the REST API Limits resource requires the Modify All Data permission.
questions.x: The Limits resource, which returns each org allocation with its maximum and remaining value, needs View Setup and Configuration. Modify All Data is not the required permission.

questions.t: If a REST API request's Accept header is missing or malformed, Salesforce returns the response as JSON.
questions.f: If a REST API request's Accept header is missing or malformed, Salesforce returns the response as XML.
