questions.x: The REST API supports JSON and XML, chosen with the Accept header, and falls back to JSON when that header is absent or malformed.

questions.t: In Salesforce REST API URIs, record IDs are case-sensitive, while object and field names are not.
questions.f: In Salesforce REST API URIs, object and field names are case-sensitive, while record IDs are not.
questions.x: Record IDs in a REST URI must match case exactly, but object and field names in the path are case-insensitive.

questions.t: External Change Data Capture in Salesforce Connect polls the source every 30 minutes by default, or as often as every 5 minutes.
questions.f: External Change Data Capture in Salesforce Connect polls the source every 5 minutes by default, or as often as every minute.
questions.x: External CDC, available only with the OData 4.0 and 4.01 adapters, defaults to a 30-minute polling interval that can be shortened to 5 minutes.

questions.t: Apex writes to external objects go through an asynchronous background queue, while writes from the UI and flows run synchronously.
questions.f: UI and flow writes to external objects go through an asynchronous background queue, while writes from Apex run synchronously.
questions.x: Salesforce Connect queues Apex writes in the background and runs UI and flow writes immediately. Either way the remote system executes the write and resolves conflicts.

questions.t: Saving changes to external objects and regular objects in the same transaction throws an error in Salesforce Connect.
questions.f: Changes to external objects and regular objects saved in the same transaction are committed or rolled back together in Salesforce Connect.
questions.x: External object writes are executed by the remote system, so Salesforce can't make them part of one transaction with regular records; mixing them raises an error.

questions.t: Metadata API deploy and retrieve move the full set of components named in a manifest, while push and pull use source tracking to move only changes.
questions.f: Push and pull move the full set of components named in a manifest, while Metadata API deploy and retrieve use source tracking to move only changes.
questions.x: Deploy and retrieve overwrite the target with every listed component. Push and pull rely on source tracking to move only what changed and to report conflicts.

questions.t: In Winter '27, the Salesforce Metadata API is at version 68.0.
questions.f: In Winter '27, the Salesforce Metadata API is at version 62.0.
questions.x: Winter '27 corresponds to Metadata API version 68.0. Version 62.0 belongs to an earlier release.

questions.t: Salesforce reruns customers' unit tests on each platform release to catch changes that would break their customizations.
questions.f: Salesforce reruns customers' unit tests only when the customer deploys new Apex to production, not on platform releases.
questions.x: Because the kernel and tenant metadata evolve separately, Salesforce runs customers' tests on each release to detect breaking changes. That safeguard only works if the tests exist.

questions.t: A standard index qualifies when a filter matches under 30% of the first million records and under 15% of records beyond that.
questions.f: A standard index qualifies when a filter matches under 50% of the first million records and under 25% of records beyond that.
questions.x: The Large Data Volumes guide publishes 30% and 15% as the standard-index thresholds. Custom indexes use the tighter 10% and 5% thresholds; 50% and 25% are not used.

questions.t: For AND filters, the query optimizer still uses their indexes unless one condition returns more than 20% of the object's records.
questions.f: For AND filters, the query optimizer still uses their indexes unless one condition returns more than 50% of the object's records.
questions.x: Compound AND conditions keep their indexes up to a 20% threshold per condition. OR conditions are different: every field must be indexed, with a 10% threshold.

questions.t: SystemModstamp is indexed by default but LastModifiedDate is not, so filtering on SystemModstamp is the selective choice.
questions.f: LastModifiedDate is indexed by default but SystemModstamp is not, so filtering on LastModifiedDate is the selective choice.
questions.x: SystemModstamp is among the default indexed fields, while LastModifiedDate is unindexed, which is why Trailhead recommends SystemModstamp for date-based filters.

questions.t: NIST SP 800-53 Revision 5 organizes its security and privacy controls into 20 families.
questions.f: NIST SP 800-53 Revision 5 organizes its security and privacy controls into 12 families.
questions.x: Rev. 5 has 20 control families, from Access Control to Supply Chain Risk Management. Twelve understates the catalog.

questions.t: The Low, Moderate and High control baselines are defined in the companion publication SP 800-53B, not in SP 800-53 itself.
questions.f: The Low, Moderate and High control baselines are defined in the companion publication SP 800-53A, not in SP 800-53 itself.
questions.x: SP 800-53 is the control catalog and SP 800-53B selects baselines from it. SP 800-53A holds assessment procedures, not baselines.

questions.t: Under FedRAMP, NIST Program Management (PM) controls remain the agency's responsibility rather than the cloud provider's.
questions.f: Under FedRAMP, NIST Program Management (PM) controls are discharged by the cloud provider's authorization rather than by the agency.
questions.x: A provider's FedRAMP authorization covers the baseline controls it was assessed on. PM controls, and privacy controls outside the baselines, stay with the agency.

questions.t: Platform Developer is the one exam required for both the Application Architect and the System Architect roll-up credentials.
questions.f: Platform App Builder is the one exam required for both the Application Architect and the System Architect roll-up credentials.
questions.x: Platform Developer sits in both prerequisite sets. Platform App Builder counts only toward Application Architect.

questions.t: Trailhead's Platform Developer study guide gives process automation and logic the largest weighting, at 28%.
questions.f: Trailhead's Platform Developer study guide gives user interface the largest weighting, at 28%.
questions.x: The guide weights process automation and logic at 28%, developer fundamentals at 27%, user interface at 25%, and testing, debugging and deployment at 20%.

questions.t: Application Architect has no maintenance requirement of its own; maintenance happens through its underlying certifications.
questions.f: Application Architect has its own annual maintenance module, separate from those of its underlying certifications.
questions.x: Because the credential is only a roll-up of four certifications, it is maintained at the level of those certifications, and its page states no separate requirement.

questions.t: The Salesforce Certified Technical Architect credential launched in 2011.
questions.f: The Salesforce Certified Technical Architect credential launched in 2017.
questions.x: The CTA dates from 2011, with the first ten certified that September. 2017 is when Dreamforce introduced the domain architect certifications as stepping stones.

questions.t: Salesforce introduced the domain architect certifications as stepping stones toward the CTA at Dreamforce '17.
questions.f: Salesforce introduced the domain architect certifications as stepping stones toward the CTA at Dreamforce '13.
questions.x: The domain architect certifications arrived at Dreamforce '17, creating the prerequisite ladder still used today. In 2013 the CTA had no such stepping stones.

questions.t: CTA601 is an expert-led virtual workshop from Trailhead Academy for experienced architects preparing for the CTA.
questions.f: CTA601 is a self-paced Trailhead module for new admins starting out on the architect path.
questions.x: CTA601 is a Trailhead Academy workshop led by experts and aimed at experienced architects, not a self-paced beginner module.

questions.t: Among System Architect's prerequisites, Identity and Access Management Architect is the one focused on single sign-on requirements.
questions.f: Among System Architect's prerequisites, Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect is the one focused on single sign-on requirements.
questions.x: The IAM Architect credential certifies design of solutions that meet single sign-on requirements. Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect covers release management, environments and deployment governance instead.

questions.t: Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect is the System Architect prerequisite that covers release management, environments and deployment governance.
questions.f: Integration Architect is the System Architect prerequisite that covers release management, environments and deployment governance.
questions.x: Release management and environment strategy belong to Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect. Integration Architect certifies end-to-end integration design.

questions.t: The System Architect credential page lists its four prerequisite certifications without prescribing the order in which to pass them.
questions.f: The System Architect credential page requires Integration Architect to be passed before the other three prerequisite certifications.
questions.x: No sequence is mandated; candidates choose their own order. Platform Developer is a natural first step for CTA-bound candidates since it also counts toward Application Architect.

questions.t: Record-triggered flows that share the same trigger order value run alphabetically by API name.
questions.f: Record-triggered flows that share the same trigger order value run in order of their activation date.
questions.x: Ties on a trigger order value are broken by API name. Activation date only orders flows that have no trigger order value at all.

questions.t: Trigger order values apply only to before-save and after-save flows and have no effect on asynchronous or scheduled paths.
questions.f: Trigger order values apply equally to before-save, after-save, asynchronous and scheduled paths of record-triggered flows.
questions.x: Ordering covers only before-save and after-save flows. Asynchronous and scheduled paths ignore it, and Trailhead notes asynchronous flows can't be guaranteed to run in the listed order.

questions.t: Pending scheduled-path runs don't appear in Flow Trigger Explorer; admins view and delete them on the Time-Based Automations setup page.
questions.f: Pending scheduled-path runs are viewed and deleted in Flow Trigger Explorer rather than on the Time-Based Automations setup page.
questions.x: The explorer lists flows and their order, not individual queued runs. Queued scheduled-path instances are managed from the Time-Based Automations page.

questions.t: A schedule-triggered flow runs on the org's default time zone from Company Information, not the time zone of the admin who built it.
questions.f: A schedule-triggered flow runs on the time zone of the admin who built it, not the org's default time zone from Company Information.
questions.x: Schedules follow the org's default time zone, so the builder's personal time zone setting has no effect and Company Information should be checked first.

questions.t: The 24-hour limit on schedule-triggered flow interviews is 250,000 or the org's user licenses times 200, whichever is greater.
questions.f: The 24-hour limit on schedule-triggered flow interviews is 250,000 or the org's user licenses times 200, whichever is smaller.
questions.x: The org-wide daily cap takes the greater of the two figures, so large orgs get more than 250,000 interviews. Exceeding it produces a flow error email.

questions.t: A schedule-triggered flow runs as the Default Workflow User set in Process Automation Settings.
questions.f: A schedule-triggered flow runs as the user who last activated it, regardless of Process Automation Settings.
questions.x: The running user comes from the Default Workflow User in Process Automation Settings, which therefore must be filled in before the flow can run.

questions.t: In Collaborative Forecasts, changing the forecast period type or the standard fiscal year purges all quotas and adjustments.
questions.f: In Collaborative Forecasts, changing the forecast period type or the standard fiscal year purges adjustments but keeps all quotas.
questions.x: Both quotas and adjustments are deleted when the period type or standard fiscal year changes, so these settings should be fixed before data is entered.

questions.t: With cumulative forecast rollups, the Commit Forecast amount covers Commit plus Closed opportunities.
questions.f: With cumulative forecast rollups, the Commit Forecast amount covers Commit plus Best Case opportunities.
questions.x: Cumulative rollups add the later categories in, so Commit includes Closed. Best Case sits earlier in the funnel and isn't added to Commit.

questions.t: A user takes part in Collaborative Forecasts only when Allow Forecasting is enabled on their user record.
questions.f: A user takes part in Collaborative Forecasts only when they hold the Override Forecasts permission.
questions.x: Allow Forecasting on the user record puts someone in the forecast hierarchy. Override Forecasts is a separate permission that lets owners or managers adjust totals.

questions.t: When calculating milestone target dates, business hours set on the milestone override those set on the entitlement process.
questions.f: When calculating milestone target dates, business hours set on the entitlement process override those set on the milestone.
questions.x: Target dates use the milestone's hours first, then the entitlement process's hours, and only if neither is set the case or work order's own hours.

questions.t: A milestone with the No Recurrence type fires only once per record.
questions.f: A milestone with the Independent recurrence type fires only once per record.
questions.x: No Recurrence fires once per record. Independent milestones fire whenever their criteria are met, and Sequential ones repeat in order each time criteria are met.

questions.t: A Case-type entitlement process won't run on work orders, so Field Service work orders need their own Work Order-type process.
questions.f: A Case-type entitlement process also runs on work orders, so Field Service work orders can share the same process as cases.
questions.x: Each entitlement process has a single type, Case or Work Order. Work orders need a Work Order-type process, which Trailhead advises leaving inactive until its milestones are added.

questions.t: Non-deterministic agent actions are built on Prompt Builder templates, while deterministic ones use a flow or Apex.
questions.f: Deterministic agent actions are built on Prompt Builder templates, while non-deterministic ones use a flow or Apex.
questions.x: Flows and Apex apply business logic and return consistent results. Prompt templates generate language, such as summaries, so their output is non-deterministic.

questions.t: Agent actions don't bulkify by default, and each action runs in its own transaction.
questions.f: Agent actions bulkify by default, and all actions in one conversation turn share a single transaction.
questions.x: Because actions aren't bulkified and each gets its own transaction, Apex behind them must be bulk-safe and the agent should be told to pass all records in one call.

questions.t: For an Apex-based agent action, whether an input is required comes from the Apex code, so changing it means editing the class.
questions.f: For an Apex-based agent action, whether an input is required is set only in Agentforce Builder, so changing it needs no code edit.
questions.x: The invocable method's variable definitions control which inputs are required. The builder pre-fills instructions from them, but the required setting is changed in code.

questions.t: Agent Script arithmetic supports only + and -, so multiplication or division belongs in a Flow or Apex action.
questions.f: Agent Script arithmetic supports +, -, * and /, so only modulo needs to move into a Flow or Apex action.
questions.x: Agent Script expressions are deliberately basic: addition and subtraction only. Any multiplication, division or modulo should be done in an action.

questions.t: In Agent Script, every user message begins processing at the start_agent block.
questions.f: In Agent Script, each user message begins processing at the subagent that handled the previous message.
questions.x: Each turn starts at start_agent and runs instructions top to bottom, rebuilding the prompt as variables change, rather than resuming in the last subagent.

questions.t: Atlas replaced Salesforce's earlier chain-of-thought planning design with ReAct-style reason, act and observe prompting.
questions.f: Atlas replaced Salesforce's earlier ReAct-style reason, act and observe prompting with chain-of-thought planning.
questions.x: The earlier assistant planned all steps up front with chain-of-thought, which tested poorly. Atlas moved to a ReAct loop that reasons, acts and observes repeatedly.

questions.t: In the legacy Atlas engine, the prompt for a turn includes recent conversation history, typically the last six turns.
questions.f: In the legacy Atlas engine, the prompt for a turn includes recent conversation history, typically the last twenty turns.
questions.x: The legacy engine builds each prompt from the subagent's scope, instructions and actions plus the user message and about six recent turns of history.

questions.t: With hybrid reasoning, once a subagent is chosen, its scripted actions run before the model evaluates the instructions.
questions.f: With hybrid reasoning, once a subagent is chosen, its scripted actions run only after the model has evaluated the instructions.
questions.x: Agent Script's deterministic steps execute first, and scripted transitions run again after each action, before Atlas decides its next step.

questions.t: In Agent Script, lines that begin with -> are logic instructions that run deterministically on every turn.
questions.f: In Agent Script, lines that begin with -> are prompt instructions handed to the LLM to interpret as it sees fit.
questions.x: The arrow marks logic lines that always execute, such as setting variables, running actions or branching. Natural-language prompt lines are marked with a pipe instead.

questions.t: On Account, the 20-field history tracking limit is shared between business accounts and person accounts.
questions.f: On Account, business accounts and person accounts each get their own separate 20-field history tracking limit.
questions.x: Field History Tracking allows 20 tracked fields per object, and on Account that one budget covers both business and person account fields.

questions.t: With no custom retention policy, Field Audit Trail archives field history after 18 months in production and after one month in sandboxes.
questions.f: With no custom retention policy, Field Audit Trail archives field history after 24 months in production and after six months in sandboxes.
questions.x: The default HistoryRetentionPolicy moves history into FieldHistoryArchive after 18 months in production and one month in sandboxes; a custom policy is deployed through Metadata API.

questions.t: To avoid parent-child data skew, Salesforce suggests no parent should hold 10,000 or more child records, using several placeholder parents if needed.
questions.f: To avoid parent-child data skew, Salesforce suggests no parent should hold 100,000 or more child records, using several placeholder parents if needed.
questions.x: The large-data-volume guidance sets the parent-child threshold at 10,000 children, spreading children across placeholder parents when no natural parent exists. 100,000 is ten times too high.

questions.t: In Bulk API 2.0, batch errors push processing into single-row mode, which sharply slows the job, so data should be cleaned first.
questions.f: In Bulk API 2.0, batch errors cause the whole job to be rejected at once, so data should be cleaned first.
questions.x: Errors don't abort the job; they drop processing to one row at a time, which is why cleaning data before a bulk load matters for speed.

questions.t: For an initial data load, Salesforce advises creating roles before sharing rules and placing users in roles before loading their records.
questions.f: For an initial data load, Salesforce advises creating sharing rules before roles and loading records before placing users in roles.
questions.x: Setting up roles and role membership first, then adding sharing rules one at a time, avoids repeated sharing recalculation as the data arrives.

questions.t: Lightning Data Service calls don't count against the org's API request usage, though general limits such as records returned still apply.
questions.f: Lightning Data Service calls count against the org's API request usage in the same way as external REST API calls.
questions.x: LDS runs on User Interface API but its calls aren't counted as API usage, so it doesn't draw down API request limits. Other platform limits still apply.

questions.t: Each Lightning Data Service adapter or function call is its own transaction, so multi-record operations through LDS aren't atomic.
questions.f: Lightning Data Service groups the adapter and function calls on a page into one transaction, so multi-record operations are atomic.
questions.x: Because each LDS call commits separately, an all-or-nothing multi-record change needs Apex, which can roll everything back on failure.

questions.t: After imperative Apex changes records, calling notifyRecordUpdateAvailable(recordIds) makes Lightning Data Service refetch them.
questions.f: After imperative Apex changes records, calling refreshApex() makes Lightning Data Service refetch them.
questions.x: LDS doesn't manage Apex results, so it must be told which records changed. refreshApex() refreshes wired Apex, and using it for non-Apex adapters is deprecated.

questions.t: The Platform Developer exam has a time limit of 105 minutes.
questions.f: The Platform Developer exam has a time limit of 120 minutes.
questions.x: Per the exam guide, candidates get 105 minutes for 60 scored questions plus up to five unscored ones. 120 minutes is not the stated limit.

questions.t: The passing score for the Platform Developer exam is 68%.
questions.f: The passing score for the Platform Developer exam is 72%.
questions.x: The exam guide sets the passing score at 68%. 72% is higher than required.

questions.t: Platform Developer and Platform Developer II share a single annual maintenance badge on the Winter cycle.
questions.f: Platform Developer and Platform Developer II share a single annual maintenance badge on the Summer cycle.
questions.x: Both credentials are maintained by one Platform Developer badge on the Winter cycle; missing it can expire the credentials tied to it, including roll-up architect credentials.

questions.t: Values that Apex or Flow write into tracked fields while a record is being created are included in its field history creation entry.
questions.f: Values that Apex or Flow write into tracked fields while a record is being created appear in field history only after a user later edits those fields.
questions.x: Record creation logs a single created entry. Typed-in values aren't logged as changes, but values automation sets during the create transaction are captured in that entry.

questions.t: A Developer Edition org gets a flat daily API request allocation of 15,000 calls.
questions.f: A Developer Edition org gets a flat daily API request allocation of 100,000 calls.
questions.x: Developer Edition has a fixed 15,000-call allocation. The 100,000 figure is the base that paid editions start from before per-license amounts are added.

questions.t: A full Salesforce license adds 1,000 daily API calls in Enterprise Edition but 5,000 in Unlimited and Performance editions.
questions.f: A full Salesforce license adds 5,000 daily API calls in Enterprise Edition but 1,000 in Unlimited and Performance editions.
questions.x: Per-license API amounts grow with the edition: 1,000 per full license in Enterprise and Professional, 5,000 in Unlimited and Performance.

questions.t: Production orgs allow up to 25 concurrent long-running API requests, meaning inbound calls lasting 20 seconds or more.
questions.f: Production orgs allow up to 100 concurrent long-running API requests, meaning inbound calls lasting 20 seconds or more.
questions.x: The concurrency cap on calls of 20 seconds or longer is 25 in production and sandboxes, and 5 in Developer Edition and trial orgs. Shorter calls have no concurrency cap.

questions.t: Salesforce's batch synchronization guidance gives Composite Graph API limits of 75 graphs per payload and 500 nodes per graph.
questions.f: Salesforce's batch synchronization guidance gives Composite Graph API limits of 500 graphs per payload and 75 nodes per graph.
questions.x: A Composite Graph payload can hold up to 75 graphs, each with up to 500 nodes. The false statement swaps the two numbers.

questions.t: Bulk API 2.0 processes batches in parallel with no serial mode, so record ordering across batches isn't guaranteed.
questions.f: Bulk API 2.0 offers a serial processing mode that guarantees record ordering across batches.
questions.x: Bulk API 2.0 always runs batches in parallel and commits each independently. Ordering isn't guaranteed and parallelism can raise lock contention.

questions.t: In batch synchronization, an ETL job's control tables should live where the ETL tool can still reach them when Salesforce is unavailable.
questions.f: In batch synchronization, an ETL job's control tables should live in Salesforce custom objects so every run reads them from the org.
questions.x: The guidance makes the ETL infrastructure the hub and Salesforce a spoke, so the job's last-run and restart data must survive a Salesforce outage.

questions.t: In the Data Virtualization pattern, the integration is always started by an event on the Salesforce side, such as a user action or search.
questions.f: In the Data Virtualization pattern, the integration is always started by an event in the external system, such as a source record change.
questions.x: Virtual integration is synchronous and initiated from Salesforce: a user action, a search or a record update triggers the live query to the source.

questions.t: Enterprise Edition's default platform event publishing allocation is 250,000 events per rolling hour.
questions.f: Enterprise Edition's default platform event publishing allocation is 50,000 events per rolling hour.
questions.x: Performance, Unlimited, Enterprise and Professional (with API add-on) all default to 250,000 published events per hour. The 50,000 figure is the Developer Edition default.

questions.t: An Apex trigger subscribed to a platform event does not use the daily event delivery allocation, but a Pub/Sub API client does.
questions.f: A Pub/Sub API client subscribed to a platform event does not use the daily event delivery allocation, but an Apex trigger does.
questions.x: The delivery allocation counts only API-based subscribers such as Pub/Sub API, CometD, empApi and event relays. Triggers, flows and processes consume no delivery allocation, so the false statement reverses the two.

questions.t: When the hourly publishing allocation is exceeded, the publish call fails with LIMIT_EXCEEDED and the event is neither published nor queued.
questions.f: When the hourly publishing allocation is exceeded, the publish call returns LIMIT_EXCEEDED and the event is queued for publishing once usage drops.
questions.x: Over the publishing allocation the event is simply rejected; nothing holds it for later, so the publisher must retry. No automatic queueing happens.

questions.t: Rolling back to an Apex savepoint undoes later DML, but static variables keep the values they had before the rollback.
questions.f: Rolling back to an Apex savepoint undoes later DML and also restores static variables to the values they had at the savepoint.
questions.x: Database.rollback only discards database changes and releases locks; in-memory static state such as recursion guards is untouched. The false statement wrongly claims statics are reset too.

questions.t: The allOrNone parameter on Database.insert defaults to true, so one failing record makes the whole call throw an exception.
questions.f: The allOrNone parameter on Database.insert defaults to false, so valid records save and failures come back as SaveResult errors.
questions.x: By default Database methods behave like plain DML and abort on the first failing record. Partial success with SaveResult errors happens only when allOrNone is explicitly set to false.

questions.t: In current API versions, each Database.setSavepoint call counts against the DML statement limit but not the DML row limit.
questions.f: In current API versions, each Database.setSavepoint call counts against the DML row limit but not the DML statement limit.
questions.x: Savepoints and rollbacks each use one DML statement from the 150-statement allowance; since API 60.0 they no longer consume DML rows. The false statement swaps the two limits.

questions.t: Under FIPS 199, a system's rating for each security objective is the highest rating among the information types it handles.
questions.f: Under FIPS 199, a system's rating for each security objective is the average rating across the information types it handles.
questions.x: Categorization uses a high-water mark per objective: the most sensitive information type sets the level. Averaging would let one critical data type be under-protected.

questions.t: In FIPS 199, a Moderate impact level means a security loss would have a serious adverse effect, and High means a severe or catastrophic one.
questions.f: In FIPS 199, a Moderate impact level means a security loss would have a limited adverse effect, and High means a serious one.
questions.x: FIPS 199 maps Low to limited, Moderate to serious and High to severe or catastrophic effects. The false statement shifts each level down by one.

questions.t: A cloud provider's FIPS 199 categorization does not replace the agency's own: each agency must categorize the data it puts in that environment.
questions.f: A cloud provider's FIPS 199 categorization replaces the agency's own, so agencies need not categorize the data they put in that environment.
questions.x: The provider categorizes its offering, but every agency still performs its own analysis of its data, and that analysis decides which authorized environment it needs.

questions.t: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 organizes its outcomes under six Functions, adding Govern to Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
questions.f: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 organizes its outcomes under five Functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
questions.x: CSF 2.0, published in February 2024, has six Functions, with Govern alongside the original five. Listing only five misses the governance function.

questions.t: An organization claiming ISO/IEC 27001:2022 conformity may not exclude any of the requirements in Clauses 4 to 10.
questions.f: An organization claiming ISO/IEC 27001:2022 conformity may exclude requirements in Clauses 4 to 10 that it judges irrelevant to its scope.
questions.x: The management-system requirements in Clauses 4 to 10 are mandatory in full for a conformity claim. Picking and choosing among them is not allowed.

questions.t: Salesforce's FedRAMP authorization covers Government Cloud Plus and MuleSoft Government Cloud, not the commercial multi-tenant platform.
questions.f: Salesforce's FedRAMP authorization covers the commercial multi-tenant platform as well as Government Cloud Plus and MuleSoft Government Cloud.
questions.x: The Trust guide limits FedRAMP scope to the government environments. Commercial orgs are outside it, so architects must check scope per service before promising FedRAMP.

questions.t: A user who can see a child opportunity, case or contact gets read-only access to its parent account through parent implicit sharing.
questions.f: A user who can see a child opportunity, case or contact gets read/write access to its parent account through parent implicit sharing.
questions.x: Parent implicit sharing is view-only: the user can open the account but not edit it. Edit access to the account needs some other grant.

questions.t: The access an account owner gets to the account's child contacts, opportunities and cases is set on the owner's role in the role hierarchy.
questions.f: The access an account owner gets to the account's child contacts, opportunities and cases is set on the account's organization-wide default.
questions.x: Child implicit sharing levels (View, Edit or No access) are defined per child object when the role is set up. The organization-wide default does not configure this owner access.

questions.t: Access to a parent account in an account hierarchy does not flow down to its child accounts; only role and territory hierarchies propagate access.
questions.f: Access to a parent account in an account hierarchy flows down to its child accounts, just as the role and territory hierarchies propagate access.
questions.x: The account hierarchy is not a sharing hierarchy, so seeing a parent account gives nothing on its child accounts. Only the role and territory hierarchies pass access along.

questions.t: A permission set group can contain at most one muting permission set.
questions.f: A permission set group can contain up to five muting permission sets.
questions.x: Each group allows a single muting permission set, which disables chosen permissions for that group only. There is no allowance for several muting sets.

questions.t: A permission muted in a permission set group is still granted to users who get it from their profile or a directly assigned permission set.
questions.f: A permission muted in a permission set group is removed from the user even if they also get it from their profile or a directly assigned permission set.
questions.x: Muting only affects what flows through that group; it is not a deny rule. Any other source of the same permission still grants it.

questions.t: In an Apex test, Test.calculatePermissionSetGroup() forces a group's recalculation so the test can assign it, and the call counts against CPU limits.
questions.f: In an Apex test, Test.calculatePermissionSetGroup() forces a group's recalculation so the test can assign it, and the call is exempt from CPU limits.
questions.x: Recalculation in tests consumes Apex CPU time, so large groups can push a test over the limit. Salesforce suggests calculating once in @testSetup and reusing it.

questions.t: Salesforce places no cap on the number of queues an org can create, and each queue gets its own list view named after its label.
questions.f: Salesforce caps an org at 50 queues, and each queue gets its own list view named after its label.
questions.x: There is no queue limit per org; every queue simply gets a list view where members see the records it owns. The 50-queue cap is invented.

questions.t: Records owned by a queue are routed only to the queue's members, never to their managers, even when those managers can see the records.
questions.f: Records owned by a queue are routed to the queue's members and also to their role-hierarchy managers when Grant Access Using Hierarchies is on.
questions.x: Grant Access Using Hierarchies only gives managers visibility. Work assignment and routing go to members alone.

questions.t: Creating or editing queues requires the Customize Application and Manage Public List Views permissions.
questions.f: Creating or editing queues requires the Manage Users and Manage Public Groups permissions.
questions.x: Customize Application plus Manage Public List Views lets an admin create and edit queues. Manage Users is needed only to edit queues created by someone else.

questions.t: One yearly Architect maintenance badge maintains all five Salesforce domain architect credentials.
questions.f: Each of the five Salesforce domain architect credentials needs its own yearly maintenance badge.
questions.x: Data, Development Lifecycle and Deployment, Identity and Access Management, Integration, and Sharing and Visibility architects share a single Architect badge, so a holder of several completes it once.

questions.t: A holder of a retired Salesforce certification keeps a valid credential, shown as retired on their profile, but loses the downloadable certificate.
questions.f: A holder of a retired Salesforce certification loses the credential at retirement unless they pass the named successor exam.
questions.x: Retirement removes maintenance and ends downloadable certificates, yet the credential stays valid and is marked retired. No successor exam is needed to keep it.

questions.t: Salesforce Foundations certifications need no maintenance badges and never expire.
questions.f: Salesforce Foundations certifications need one maintenance badge a year and expire if it is missed.
questions.x: Foundations credentials are an exception to the yearly maintenance rule and do not expire. Other certifications expire when their yearly badge is missed.

questions.t: An org can keep several case assignment rules, but only one case assignment rule can be active at a time.
questions.f: An org can keep several case assignment rules, and up to five case assignment rules can be active at a time.
questions.x: Each of leads and cases allows exactly one active rule; alternates such as a holiday rule are kept inactive and swapped in. Multiple active rules are not possible.

questions.t: A case assignment rule can contain up to 3,000 rule entries, of which up to 300 can be formula entries.
questions.f: A case assignment rule can contain up to 300 rule entries, of which up to 30 can be formula entries.
questions.x: The cap is 3,000 entries per case assignment rule, with 300 of them allowed to use formulas. The false statement divides both numbers by ten.

questions.t: If an org has no assignment rules, leads or cases saved via API version 30.0 or later stay unassigned rather than getting a default owner.
questions.f: If an org has no assignment rules, leads or cases saved via API version 30.0 or later are given a predefined default owner.
questions.x: From API 30.0 the record is left unassigned when no rules exist. Assigning a predefined default owner was the behaviour for API 29.0 and earlier.

questions.t: A platform event-triggered flow interview runs in the context of the user who published the event, so created records show that publisher in CreatedById.
questions.f: A platform event-triggered flow interview runs as the Automated Process user, so created records show Automated Process in CreatedById.
questions.x: Only the debug logs go under Automated Process; the interview itself runs as the publishing user. Running as Automated Process is the default for platform event Apex triggers, not flows.

questions.t: A platform event-triggered flow can receive up to 200 event messages in one batch, keeping their order within the batch.
questions.f: A platform event-triggered flow can receive up to 2,000 event messages in one batch, keeping their order within the batch.
questions.x: Flow subscribers get batches of at most 200 messages, processed in replay ID order. The 2,000 figure is far above the flow batch size.

questions.t: When a platform event fails, the subscribed platform event-triggered flow doesn't start and no flow error email is sent.
questions.f: When a platform event fails, the subscribed platform event-triggered flow doesn't start, and a flow error email is sent to the admin.
questions.x: These failures are silent from Flow's point of view: no interview and no error email. Troubleshooting has to rely on the errors the platform event itself produces.

questions.t: Revenue splits on an opportunity are capped at 100%, while overlay splits can total more than 100%.
questions.f: Overlay splits on an opportunity are capped at 100%, while revenue splits can total more than 100%.
questions.x: Revenue splits divide credit among the people directly responsible, so they can't exceed 100%. Overlay splits credit supporting effort on top of that and may go over 100%.

questions.t: Besides the two default split types, admins can create up to 6 custom opportunity split types.
questions.f: Besides the two default split types, admins can create up to 20 custom opportunity split types.
questions.x: Salesforce allows six custom split types in addition to the default revenue and overlay types. Twenty overstates the limit.

questions.t: A custom opportunity split type can split a roll-up summary or custom currency field, but not a formula currency field.
questions.f: A custom opportunity split type can split a formula currency or custom currency field, but not a roll-up summary field.
questions.x: Standard currency, roll-up summary and custom currency fields are allowed as the basis of a custom split type; formula currency fields are the excluded kind.

questions.t: The Agentforce Sales Consultant credential lists the Salesforce Certified Platform Administrator as its prerequisite.
questions.f: The Agentforce Sales Consultant credential lists the Salesforce Certified Platform App Builder as its prerequisite.
questions.x: The credential page names Platform Administrator as the required prior certification. Platform App Builder is not the listed prerequisite.

questions.t: The Agentforce Sales Consultant credential is kept current by completing the Platform Administrator maintenance badge each year.
questions.f: The Agentforce Sales Consultant credential is kept current by completing a Sales-specific consultant maintenance badge each year.
questions.x: Rather than its own Sales badge, this credential's yearly requirement is the Platform Administrator maintenance module, which the Agentforce Service Consultant also uses.

questions.t: In the Sales Cloud Consultant exam outline used since June 2024, practical application of Sales Cloud expertise is the largest section at 33%.
questions.f: In the Sales Cloud Consultant exam outline used since June 2024, the sales lifecycle is the largest section at 33%.
questions.x: Practical application of Sales Cloud expertise carries 33% of the exam; the sales lifecycle section is next at 23%.

questions.t: Salesforce, Inc.'s fiscal year ends on January 31, so its fiscal 2026 closed on January 31, 2026.
questions.f: Salesforce, Inc.'s fiscal year ends on December 31, so its fiscal 2026 closes on December 31, 2026.
questions.x: Salesforce runs a fiscal year that ends January 31, so fiscal 2026 ended early in calendar 2026. A calendar-year fiscal year is incorrect.

questions.t: A Salesforce Winter release ships in October of the preceding calendar year, which is why it carries the next year's number.
questions.f: A Salesforce Winter release ships in January of the calendar year whose number it carries.
questions.x: Release names are seasonal rather than calendar-aligned: Winter arrives around October and is labelled with the following year. January is not when Winter ships.

questions.t: Salesforce ships three seasonal major releases a year, Spring, Summer and Winter, typically in February, June and October.
questions.f: Salesforce ships four seasonal major releases a year, Spring, Summer, Fall and Winter, typically in February, May, August and November.
questions.x: There are three major releases a year with no Fall release, landing around February, June and October. Some products also ship monthly updates in between.

questions.t: In Agentforce Builder's Preview panel, Simulate mode uses mock data without running actions, while Live Test runs real actions and changes org data.
questions.f: In Agentforce Builder's Preview panel, Live Test uses mock data without running actions, while Simulate mode runs real actions and changes org data.
questions.x: Simulate checks configuration safely with mock data and no permission enforcement. Live Test is the mode that executes actions against real records; the false statement swaps them.

questions.t: In Agentforce Builder only one version of an agent can be live, so activating a committed version deactivates the previous one.
questions.f: In Agentforce Builder several committed versions of an agent can be live at once, so activating one leaves the previous one active.
questions.x: Committed versions are locked snapshots, and only one of them is active at a time. Activating a new version automatically turns off the earlier one.

questions.t: Agentforce Session Tracing, which groups reasoning runs, action calls and errors by session ID, requires Data 360.
questions.f: Agentforce Session Tracing, which groups reasoning runs, action calls and errors by session ID, requires Shield Event Monitoring.
questions.x: Session Tracing and some other Studio observability tools depend on Data 360. Shield Event Monitoring is not the stated dependency.

questions.t: In an Agentforce Testing Center CSV, the Expected Subagent column takes the subagent's API name, not its label.
questions.f: In an Agentforce Testing Center CSV, the Expected Subagent column takes the subagent's label, not its API name.
questions.x: Test cases match subagents by API name, so entering the display label gives a mismatch. The same API-name convention applies to expected actions.

questions.t: Agentforce Testing Center can run up to 10 test jobs at once within a 10-hour window.
questions.f: Agentforce Testing Center can run up to 3 test jobs at once within a 24-hour window.
questions.x: The documented capacity is 10 concurrent test jobs in a 10-hour window. The 3-job, 24-hour figures are invented.

questions.t: Agentforce agent tests are stored as the AiEvaluationDefinition Metadata API type, which needs API version 63.0 or later.
questions.f: Agentforce agent tests are stored as the BotTestDefinition Metadata API type, which needs API version 60.0 or later.
questions.x: AiEvaluationDefinition, available from API 63.0, holds agent tests so they can be deployed between orgs and run in CI. BotTestDefinition is not the type used.

questions.t: A Salesforce support process filters the values offered in the case Status picklist.
questions.f: A Salesforce support process filters the values offered in the case Priority picklist.
questions.x: Each business process type is bound to one lifecycle field, and for support processes that field is case Status. Priority is not governed by a business process.

questions.t: A value added to an object's master picklist is not added to existing business processes; it must be added to each one by hand.
questions.f: A value added to an object's master picklist is added automatically to every existing business process on that object.
questions.x: Existing processes and record types keep their own selected values, so new master values need to be added to each manually.

questions.t: Users can still read records whose business process their profile can't create or edit, so business processes shouldn't be used for access control.
questions.f: Users can't read records whose business process their profile can't create or edit, so business processes can serve as access control.
questions.x: Profile assignment of a process governs creating and editing, not reading. Salesforce warns against relying on business processes as a security control.

questions.t: A standard object can't be the detail side of a master-detail relationship whose master is a custom object, so a lookup must be used instead.
questions.f: A standard object can be the detail side of a master-detail relationship whose master is a custom object, as long as the object has no record types.
questions.x: Standard objects such as Account or Case can't be master-detail children of a custom parent, whatever their configuration. A lookup relationship is the workaround.

questions.t: Lead is a standard object that cannot act as the master in a master-detail relationship.
questions.f: Lead is a standard object that cannot act as the detail in a lookup relationship.
questions.x: Some standard objects, Lead among them, are barred from being a master-detail parent. Nothing stops Lead from holding lookup fields.

questions.t: Every Salesforce record gets an automatically generated 18-character, case-insensitive record ID as its identity field.
questions.f: Every Salesforce record gets an automatically generated 12-character, case-sensitive record ID as its identity field.
questions.x: The identity field the API generates on create is an 18-character ID that is case-insensitive. A 12-character case-sensitive ID is not what the platform uses.

questions.t: An Aura component can contain Lightning web components, but a Lightning web component cannot contain Aura components.
questions.f: A Lightning web component can contain Aura components, but an Aura component cannot contain Lightning web components.
questions.x: Nesting only works one way: Aura can host LWC, which is why thin Aura wrappers are used. An LWC cannot embed an Aura component.

questions.t: In Aura, a component event is handled by the firing component or one above it in the containment hierarchy, while an application event reaches every registered handler.
questions.f: In Aura, an application event is handled by the firing component or one above it in the containment hierarchy, while a component event reaches every registered handler.
questions.x: Component events travel up the containment hierarchy; application events use publish-subscribe and notify all registered handlers. The false statement swaps the two.

questions.t: An Aura server action marked abortable is dropped from the queue if its component has been unrendered before it is sent.
questions.f: An Aura server action marked storable is dropped from the queue if its component has been unrendered before it is sent.
questions.x: Abortable actions are discarded when their component is gone. Storable actions are about caching: cached data renders first while fresh data is fetched.

questions.t: Salesforce doesn't guarantee the execution order of several Apex triggers on the same object for the same event, which is why one trigger per object is advised.
questions.f: Salesforce runs several Apex triggers on the same object for the same event in alphabetical order by name, which is why one trigger per object is optional.
questions.x: Multiple triggers on one object and event run in no guaranteed order, causing nondeterministic bugs. A single trigger delegating to a handler makes the order explicit in code.

questions.t: Static variables are not reset between trigger invocations within one Bulk API request, even though governor limits are reset.
questions.f: Static variables are reset between trigger invocations within one Bulk API request, just as governor limits are reset.
questions.x: Within a single Bulk API request, statics persist across trigger chunks while limits reset. Recursion guards built on static flags can therefore misbehave, which is why field-change checks are recommended.

questions.t: A metadata-driven trigger framework stores action execution order in custom metadata, so admins can reorder actions without a deployment.
questions.f: A metadata-driven trigger framework stores action execution order in custom settings data, so admins can reorder actions only through a code deployment.
questions.x: The metadata-driven flavour keeps the sequence of small action classes in custom metadata records that a central handler reads. Changing the order needs no code change.

questions.t: Retrieving the Agent:<name> pseudo type also pulls the agent's action Apex and flows, but deleting it leaves that Apex and those flows in place.
questions.f: Retrieving the Agent:<name> pseudo type also pulls the agent's action Apex and flows, and deleting it removes that Apex and those flows too.
questions.x: Agent: is a convenience pseudo type, not real metadata. Its retrieve expands to the supporting Apex and flows, but deploy and delete operations don't touch them.

questions.t: In Agentforce DX, sf agent generate test-spec writes an agent's test cases to a YAML file, chosen because it reads and diffs well in source control.
questions.f: In Agentforce DX, sf agent generate test-spec writes an agent's test cases to a CSV file, chosen because it opens directly in spreadsheet tools.
questions.x: The spec-first test flow uses YAML, which Salesforce picked for readability and clean diffs. sf agent test create then turns that spec into a test in the org.

questions.t: Running sf agent deactivate ends the agent's open conversations and makes it unreachable on every channel.
questions.f: Running sf agent deactivate lets the agent's open conversations finish while blocking new ones on every channel.
questions.x: Deactivation is immediate: active conversations are ended and the agent goes offline everywhere, so it should be handled as a production change.

questions.t: Tooling API queries on EntityDefinition or FieldDefinition silently ignore LIMIT and OFFSET, so a tool can get wrong results without any error.
questions.f: Tooling API queries on EntityDefinition or FieldDefinition reject LIMIT and OFFSET with an error, so a tool learns at once that they aren't supported.
questions.x: Metadata Catalog entities don't support several SOQL clauses; most raise errors, but LIMIT and OFFSET are dropped quietly. That silent behaviour is the trap.

questions.t: A synchronous Tooling API test run through /runTestsSynchronous/ must keep all of its test methods in a single class.
questions.f: A synchronous Tooling API test run through /runTestsSynchronous/ can include test methods from up to five classes.
questions.x: Synchronous runs are restricted to one test class; running several classes needs the asynchronous resource. The five-class allowance is invented.

questions.t: The Tooling API composite resource can bundle several Tooling API requests into one call that counts once against API limits.
questions.f: Tooling API requests don't count against the org's API limits, so bundling them with the composite resource saves nothing.
questions.x: Tooling API calls consume the org's API request allocation. The composite resource, available from API 40.0, reduces consumption by counting several requests as one.

questions.t: Headless Identity requires an Experience Cloud site, even if end users never see it, because the APIs are exposed and configured through the site.
questions.f: Headless Identity requires no Experience Cloud site, because the APIs are exposed and configured entirely through the external client app.
questions.x: The site is mandatory: it exposes and configures the headless APIs and stores the customer accounts and contacts. The client app alone isn't enough.

questions.t: Headless login, registration and passwordless flows use the Authorization Code and Credentials flow, requested with response_type=code_credentials.
questions.f: Headless login, registration and passwordless flows use the OAuth username-password flow, requested with grant_type=password.
questions.x: These flows post credentials to the authorize endpoint with response_type=code_credentials and then exchange the returned code for a token. The username-password grant isn't used.

questions.t: Headless Identity's code-and-credentials flow works only against an Experience Cloud site domain, not employee logins through a My Domain login URL.
questions.f: Headless Identity's code-and-credentials flow works against a My Domain login URL for employees as well as against Experience Cloud site domains.
questions.x: The flow is limited to site domains such as *.my.site.com and doesn't support employee login through login.salesforce.com or My Domain.

questions.t: Salesforce login flows run after the user has authenticated, including after SAML SSO, and add logic on top rather than replacing authentication.
questions.f: Salesforce login flows run before the user authenticates and replace the password or SAML SSO step with custom logic.
questions.x: A login flow is inserted after authentication succeeds and before the user reaches the org. It extends password, delegated or SSO login; it never substitutes for it.

questions.t: A login flow is assigned to a user license and profile, so only users with that profile go through it.
questions.f: A login flow is assigned to a permission set, so only users holding that permission set go through it.
questions.x: In Setup each login flow is tied to a license and profile, which lets different profiles get different flows. Permission sets aren't the assignment mechanism.

questions.t: Login flows don't run for API logins, so controls that must cover integrations need to live elsewhere.
questions.f: Login flows run for API logins as well as UI logins, so they can enforce controls on integrations too.
questions.x: API logins, and UI sessions created via frontdoor.jsp from a non-UI login, bypass login flows. Integration controls belong in places such as connected-app policies.

questions.t: For a multi-org enterprise, Salesforce recommends a single Data Cloud Home Org with the other orgs attached as companion orgs.
questions.f: For a multi-org enterprise, Salesforce recommends a separate Data Cloud instance in every production org, each kept independent.
questions.x: The provisioning guide favours one Home Org hosting Data Cloud, with companion orgs connected. Separate instances are reserved for strict autonomy, residency or compliance needs.

questions.t: Under the operating-model framework, highly standardized and integrated businesses favour as few Salesforce orgs as possible.
questions.f: Under the operating-model framework, highly diversified businesses with little shared process favour as few Salesforce orgs as possible.
questions.x: Standardized, integrated operating models gain most from consolidation. Diversified businesses with little common process are the ones likely to keep several orgs.

questions.t: Since the December 2025 refresh, Data and Analytics Management is the heaviest section of the Platform Administrator exam at 17%.
questions.f: Since the December 2025 refresh, Automation is the heaviest section of the Platform Administrator exam at 17%.
questions.x: Data and Analytics Management carries 17%, the largest single weight. Automation sits at 15%, alongside Configuration and Setup and Object Manager.

questions.t: The December 2025 Platform Administrator exam refresh added an Agentforce section weighted at 8%, without expecting expert-level Agentforce knowledge.
questions.f: The December 2025 Platform Administrator exam refresh added an Agentforce section weighted at 20%, expecting expert-level Agentforce knowledge.
questions.x: Agentforce is the smallest section at 8%, and the Admins blog says expert depth isn't expected. The 20% weight and expert framing are wrong.

questions.t: Platform Administrator II lists the Platform Administrator certification as its prerequisite, so a lapse in the base credential undermines it.
questions.f: Platform Administrator II lists Platform App Builder as its prerequisite, so a lapse in the Platform Administrator credential doesn't affect it.
questions.x: The advanced admin credential builds on Platform Administrator, not App Builder, so keeping the base credential maintained matters for both.

questions.t: A skinny table is created only by Salesforce Customer Support on request; customers cannot create, access or modify one themselves.
questions.f: A skinny table is created by an admin from a Skinny Tables page in Setup, where its field list can later be edited.
questions.x: There is no setup page: Support builds the table and the platform uses it automatically. Changing its fields also needs a Support request.

questions.t: A skinny table can't include fields from other objects, so a query that needs a parent object's fields can't be served from it alone.
questions.f: A skinny table can include fields from parent objects reached through lookups, so it can serve queries that span related objects.
questions.x: Each skinny table holds fields from one object only; cross-object fields are not allowed. That is why it removes the standard/custom field join but not joins across objects.

questions.t: Skinny tables leave out soft-deleted records in the Recycle Bin, which can shrink the volume a query scans.
questions.f: Skinny tables keep soft-deleted records from the Recycle Bin alongside live rows, so a query scans the same volume as the base table.
questions.x: Excluding soft-deleted rows is one of the reasons skinny tables speed up reads, alongside narrower rows and avoiding the standard/custom field join.

questions.t: CJIS compliance is audited at the agency level by the state's CJIS Systems Agency, unlike FedRAMP, which authorizes a cloud offering centrally.
questions.f: CJIS compliance is granted centrally to a cloud offering by the FBI, just as FedRAMP authorizes a cloud offering centrally.
questions.x: There is no central CJIS authorization for a product. Each state CSA audits its agencies, and vendors supply independent assessments that customers build on.

questions.t: CJIS Security Policy v6.0 requires a device session lock after at most 30 minutes of inactivity.
questions.f: CJIS Security Policy v6.0 requires a device session lock after at most 120 minutes of inactivity.
questions.x: Control AC-11 caps inactivity before session lock at 30 minutes. Two hours is far longer than the policy allows.

questions.t: CJIS Security Policy v6.0 requires audit records to be kept for at least one year.
questions.f: CJIS Security Policy v6.0 requires audit records to be kept for at least ninety days.
questions.x: Control AU-11 sets audit record retention at a minimum of one year. Ninety days is the account-inactivity threshold, not the retention period.

questions.t: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 consolidated the 114 controls of the 2013 edition into 93 controls.
questions.f: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 expanded the 93 controls of the 2013 edition into 114 controls.
questions.x: The 2022 revision reduced and regrouped the catalog, going from 114 controls to 93 in new Clauses 5 to 8. The false statement reverses the direction.

questions.t: The deadline for moving an ISO/IEC 27001:2013 certification to the 2022 edition was 31 October 2025.
questions.f: The deadline for moving an ISO/IEC 27001:2013 certification to the 2022 edition is 31 October 2027.
questions.x: Organizations had a 36-month transition ending 31 October 2025, after which 2013-based certificates expire or are withdrawn.

questions.t: ISO/IEC 27001 is delivered as a certificate against a management-system standard, whereas SOC 2 is delivered as an audit report.
questions.f: ISO/IEC 27001 is delivered as an audit report on controls, whereas SOC 2 is delivered as a certificate against a management-system standard.
questions.x: An accredited body certifies an ISMS to ISO/IEC 27001, while SOC 1 and SOC 2 take the form of attestation reports. The false statement swaps the two forms.

questions.t: In a Field Audit Trail retention policy, archiveRetentionYears is only a reminder; archived history is never deleted automatically.
questions.f: In a Field Audit Trail retention policy, archived history is deleted automatically once archiveRetentionYears has elapsed.
questions.x: The setting records an intended retention period but triggers no purge. Orgs that must destroy data after a period need their own scheduled deletion job.

questions.t: Deleting a production record removes its live field history but leaves its Field Audit Trail archive rows until they are purged.
questions.f: Deleting a production record removes both its live field history and its Field Audit Trail archive rows.
questions.x: Archived copies in FieldHistoryArchive survive record deletion; removing them needs an explicit deleteByExample() or Database.deleteImmediate() call with the right permissions.

questions.t: To delete FieldHistoryArchive rows, the template record must supply every field in the big object's index; partial indexes and wildcards are rejected.
questions.f: To delete FieldHistoryArchive rows, the template record may supply a partial index or wildcards to match many rows at once.
questions.x: Archive deletion via deleteByExample() or Database.deleteImmediate() follows big-object index rules, so the full index must be given. Partial or wildcard templates fail.

questions.t: Salesforce's org strategy guidance says apparent platform limit problems should be raised with the account team before they drive an org split.
questions.f: Salesforce's org strategy guidance says apparent platform limit problems are the clearest signal that a single org should be split into several.
questions.x: The guidance cautions against splitting orgs reactively over limits; such issues go to the account team first. Org splits should follow the business, technology, governance and operations factors.

questions.t: Shield Platform Encryption becomes available in sandboxes only after it has been provisioned for the production org.
questions.f: Shield Platform Encryption can be provisioned in a sandbox for testing before it has been provisioned for the production org.
questions.x: Sandbox availability follows the production licence, so rehearsals happen once production is provisioned. A sandbox-first trial isn't how it is enabled.

questions.t: Shield Platform Encryption requires deterministic encryption for custom fields marked Unique or External ID.
questions.f: Shield Platform Encryption requires probabilistic encryption for custom fields marked Unique or External ID.
questions.x: Unique and External ID custom fields must be matched on exact values, so they need the deterministic scheme. Probabilistic is the default for ordinary fields but can't serve these.

questions.t: In a production org, a new Probabilistic tenant secret for Shield Platform Encryption can be generated only once every 24 hours.
questions.f: In a production org, a new Probabilistic tenant secret for Shield Platform Encryption can be generated only once every 7 days.
questions.x: Production orgs may generate a fresh Probabilistic tenant secret once per 24 hours, not once per week. Each secret type is also capped at 50 active and archived secrets.

questions.t: Enabling Shield Platform Encryption encrypts only data created or updated afterward; existing values need a sync or background encryption process.
questions.f: Enabling Shield Platform Encryption immediately encrypts all existing values of the selected fields, along with any data created afterward.
questions.x: Encryption applies going forward only. Values already stored are brought into line through the Encryption Statistics and Data Sync pages or a background process, not automatically at enablement.

questions.t: Salesforce Architects launched the decision guides in June 2020 with two titles: one on building forms and one on record-triggered automation.
questions.f: Salesforce Architects launched the decision guides in June 2020 with two titles: one on event-driven architecture and one on data integration.
questions.x: The first two guides covered building forms and record-triggered automation. Event-driven architecture and data integration guides came later and were updated in subsequent change announcements.

questions.t: The Orchestration Density framework, which scores execution path, goal complexity and modality mix, comes from the Agentic and Traditional Workflow Automation guide.
questions.f: The Orchestration Density framework, which scores execution path, goal complexity and modality mix, comes from the Asynchronous Processing decision guide.
questions.x: Orchestration Density is how the agentic versus traditional automation guide maps low, medium and high density to tools from Flow and Apex up to Agentforce and MuleSoft. The Asynchronous Processing guide instead compares Queueable, Scheduled Apex, platform event triggers, CDC and async flow paths.

questions.t: The event-driven architecture decision guide says Salesforce will keep supporting PushTopic and generic events without further investment and recommends moving to Pub/Sub API.
questions.f: The event-driven architecture decision guide says Salesforce will keep supporting PushTopic and generic events without further investment and recommends moving to Outbound Messages.
questions.x: The guide signals that PushTopic and generic events are supported but no longer invested in, and points teams to Pub/Sub API where feasible. Outbound Messages are just another option compared in the guide, not the recommended successor.

questions.t: Whether a Salesforce Holiday record recurs can be set only when the holiday is created, not changed afterwards.
questions.f: Whether a Salesforce Holiday record recurs can be switched on or off at any time after the holiday is created.
questions.x: The Holiday object fixes the recurring setting at creation; only then can you choose it. Toggling recurrence later on an existing holiday isn't possible, so a new record is needed instead.

questions.t: In Apex, BusinessHours.addGmt returns a GMT datetime, while BusinessHours.add returns a datetime in local time.
questions.f: In Apex, BusinessHours.add returns a GMT datetime, while BusinessHours.addGmt returns a datetime in local time.
questions.x: The add and nextStartDate methods give local-time results and addGmt gives GMT. Swapping them, as the false statement does, is exactly the kind of mix-up that causes time-zone offset bugs in SLA code.

questions.t: Change sets don't support business hours on entitlement processes, so the process must be recreated, deployed another way, or stripped of its hours first.
questions.f: Change sets fully support business hours on entitlement processes, so the process deploys with its hours intact like any other component.
questions.x: Salesforce lists business hours on entitlement processes as unsupported in change sets. Its workarounds are recreating the process in the target org, using another deployment method, or removing the hours before packaging.

questions.t: Each case escalation rule entry can have up to five escalation actions, each firing at a longer case age.
questions.f: Each case escalation rule entry can have up to ten escalation actions, each firing at a longer case age.
questions.x: Salesforce allows a maximum of five timed escalation actions per rule entry, set over increasing Age Over periods. Ten exceeds that cap.

questions.t: With the escalation clock set to start at case creation but disable once the case is first modified, any edit permanently stops escalation for that case.
questions.f: With the escalation clock set to start at case creation but disable once the case is first modified, any edit restarts the escalation clock from zero.
questions.x: The disable-after-first-modified option switches escalation off for the case after any change, even a trivial one. Restarting the clock on every edit is the separate last-modified option.

questions.t: In the save order of execution, escalation rules are evaluated right after workflow rules and before Salesforce Flow automations.
questions.f: In the save order of execution, escalation rules are evaluated right after Salesforce Flow automations and before workflow rules.
questions.x: Escalation rules sit at step 12, following workflow rules and preceding the flow automations at step 13. The false version reverses their position relative to workflow rules and flows.

questions.t: By default, anyone who can open a CRM Analytics dataset sees all of its rows, so row-level security must be added per dataset.
questions.f: By default, CRM Analytics datasets enforce each user's Salesforce record access, so row-level security needs no per-dataset setup.
questions.x: Datasets are copies that don't inherit org record access on their own. Admins must add security predicates or sharing inheritance to each dataset to restrict rows.

questions.t: Einstein Discovery requires a CRM Analytics Plus license or an Einstein Predictions license.
questions.f: Einstein Discovery is included with a CRM Analytics Growth license with no further licensing needed.
questions.x: Of the two CRM Analytics licenses, only Plus covers Einstein Discovery; otherwise an Einstein Predictions license is needed. Growth alone doesn't include it.

questions.t: CRM Analytics sharing inheritance supports Accounts, Cases, Contacts, Leads and Opportunities as source objects.
questions.f: CRM Analytics sharing inheritance supports any standard or custom object as a source object.
questions.x: Sharing inheritance is limited to five objects: Accounts, Cases, Contacts, Leads and Opportunities. It is not offered for every standard or custom object.

questions.t: In Data 360, an ensemble retriever combines several individual retrievers, merges their results and reranks them by relevance.
questions.f: In Data 360, a custom SQL retriever combines several individual retrievers, merges their results and reranks them by relevance.
questions.x: Merging and reranking results from multiple individual retrievers is the job of an ensemble retriever. A custom SQL retriever instead runs a parameterized SQL query against Data 360 objects.

questions.t: Data 360 retrievers follow data governance policies, so records the running user or agent can't access are left out of the results.
questions.f: Data 360 retrievers return every indexed record, and record access is enforced afterwards only by the Einstein Trust Layer.
questions.x: Retrievers are permission-aware and drop records the user or agent can't see. The Einstein Trust Layer adds prompt-level safeguards but is not what filters retrieval results by record access.

questions.t: A hybrid search index in Data 360 combines semantic vector similarity with keyword matching.
questions.f: A hybrid search index in Data 360 combines semantic vector similarity with SQL filters on structured fields.
questions.x: Data 360 offers vector search and hybrid search, and hybrid adds keyword matching to semantic similarity. Querying structured data with SQL is what a custom SQL retriever does, not a hybrid index.

questions.t: A field marked required on a page layout but read-only in field-level security is read-only for the user.
questions.f: A field marked required on a page layout but read-only in field-level security is required and editable for the user.
questions.x: Field-level security overrides any less restrictive layout setting, so the stricter read-only access wins. The layout's required flag can't open up editing that FLS denies.

questions.t: In Lightning Experience, the highlights panel on a record page takes its fields from the object's compact layout.
questions.f: In Lightning Experience, the highlights panel on a record page takes its fields from the object's page layout.
questions.x: The compact layout supplies the highlights panel fields. The page layout still provides the related lists, buttons, links and quick actions rendered on the Lightning page.

questions.t: When a new custom field is added to a page layout, it lands by default as the last field in the layout's first section.
questions.f: When a new custom field is added to a page layout, it lands by default as the first field in the layout's last section.
questions.x: Salesforce places a newly added custom field at the end of the first section, where admins can then drag it elsewhere. It is not dropped at the top of the last section.

questions.t: On tasks and events, the WhoId field is labelled Name in the UI and points to a person such as a Lead or a Contact.
questions.f: On tasks and events, the WhatId field is labelled Name in the UI and points to a person such as a Lead or a Contact.
questions.x: Who (WhoId, shown as Name) is the person an activity concerns. What (WhatId, shown as Related To) points to non-person records such as Accounts or Opportunities.

questions.t: With Shared Activities enabled, a single task or event can be related to up to 50 contacts, one of which is the primary contact.
questions.f: With Shared Activities enabled, a single task or event can be related to up to 10 contacts, one of which is the primary contact.
questions.x: Shared Activities lets one activity relate to as many as 50 contacts with one marked primary. The limit is 50, not 10, and turning the setting off requires Salesforce Support.

questions.t: TYPEOF can't be used in Bulk API queries, so large extracts of polymorphic fields filter on the Type qualifier instead.
questions.f: The Type qualifier can't be used in Bulk API queries, so large extracts of polymorphic fields use TYPEOF instead.
questions.x: TYPEOF is unsupported in Bulk API and PushTopic queries, so bulk extracts rely on filters like What.Type. The false statement reverses which construct is blocked.

questions.t: If the transaction that queued a future method rolls back, the future job is never processed.
questions.f: If the transaction that queued a future method rolls back, the future job still runs because it was already queued.
questions.x: Future work queued by a transaction is discarded if that transaction rolls back, so the job never executes. It does not run independently of the transaction that queued it.

questions.t: Future method executions draw on the same 24-hour async Apex allowance that Batch, Queueable and scheduled Apex also consume.
questions.f: Future method executions draw on their own 24-hour allowance, separate from the one Batch, Queueable and scheduled Apex consume.
questions.x: The org has one shared daily allowance for asynchronous Apex executions, and future methods count against it with the other async types. There is no separate future-only pool.

questions.t: A future method can't call another future method, so code checks System.isFuture() and skips the call when already in a future context.
questions.f: A future method can call one more future method, so code checks System.isFuture() and skips the call once a second level is reached.
questions.x: Future and batch contexts can make no future calls at all, so any chaining attempt fails. System.isFuture() detects the future context so code can avoid the call entirely.

questions.t: A single-object SOSL search returns up to 250 records unless a WHERE or ORDER BY clause is added, which raises the cap to 2,000.
questions.f: A single-object SOSL search returns up to 2,000 records unless a WHERE or ORDER BY clause is added, which lowers the cap to 250.
questions.x: The default per-object cap for a single-object search is 250, and adding WHERE or ORDER BY lifts it to 2,000. The false statement inverts the default and the effect of the clauses.

questions.t: An Apex transaction can run at most 20 SOSL queries, whether it is synchronous or asynchronous.
questions.f: An Apex transaction can run at most 100 SOSL queries, whether it is synchronous or asynchronous.
questions.x: Apex governor limits allow 20 SOSL queries per transaction in both contexts. 100 is the SOQL figure for synchronous code, not the SOSL limit.

questions.t: A SOSL search string longer than 4,000 characters silently drops its logical operators, so AND can behave like OR.
questions.f: A SOSL search string longer than 4,000 characters silently drops its wildcards, so * and ? are matched as literal characters.
questions.x: Past 4,000 characters SOSL ignores logical operators, which can broaden a search unexpectedly. The documented loss is of AND/OR logic, not of wildcard handling.

questions.t: A managed package namespace prefix can be up to 15 alphanumeric characters, must start with a letter and can't contain two consecutive underscores.
